index.html.index.001: Firmware, or the present state of local reality. This handbook describes v3.0x. Its menu pages, clock colours and encoder tables belong to that firmware generation. Other generations may have developed opinions of their own.
index.html.index.002: For questions about an order, write to info@toern.live. If the handbook and the unit disagree, record the disagreement in an issue on GitHub. This gives the next revision something useful to feel embarrassed about.
index.html.index.003: TŒRN is a sampler and step sequencer: a small rectangle in which time has agreed to travel left to right. Voices stack upward on its RGB LED grid, which also serves as the display. Four rotary encoders let you draw, sculpt and arrange events with considerably less paperwork than the universe normally requires. A Micro SD card supplies eight sample lanes for drums and one-shots; a three-voice synth and two mono synths handle melodic matters. You can record directly on the device, should reality produce a noise worth keeping.
index.html.index.004: This handbook begins where the delivery ends. While waiting for your TŒRN, you can meet its simulator, which is unusually patient about being misunderstood. Begin with Your first beat in 1 minute, then read onward. USB-C provides power; the SD card chapter explains the card. Readers already on speaking terms with the machine can head for the screen index or menu map.
index.html.index.005: How to find your way through this part of the universe
index.html.index.006: The sidebar divides the expedition into three groups. This is fewer than most expeditions require, and considerably easier to find your way home from:
index.html.index.007: Get started — make a beat in a minute, then inspect the hardware, matrix and controls. Establishing what the objects are before operating them is a useful local custom.
index.html.index.008: Compose — sequencing, pages, advanced tools, samples, sound design, the audio path, recording and note detail. This is where the noises acquire intentions.
index.html.index.009: Operate — tempo and MIDI, song mode, saving and the full menu: the practicalities of sharing a studio with a small electronic personality. Includes the screen index and troubleshooting, for when introductions go poorly.
index.html.index.010: Where a display matters, the chapter shows it. Encoder tables provide one column per knob, a rare case in which the number of explanations matches the number of objects being explained. Destructive and easily missed gestures have callouts. Links lead to the menu map and screen index whenever a feature has acquired a page of its own.

first-beat.html.first-beat.001: Your first beat, pending the cooperation of time
first-beat.html.first-beat.002: Seven steps from a fresh TŒRN to a beat. The minute is an estimate; time has never been especially reliable when somebody is watching it.
first-beat.html.first-beat.004: Flip the side switch. Once the boot animation has finished introducing itself, you arrive in draw mode: a mostly dark grid with a dim band in each voice lane’s colour on rows 2–15. This is readiness, rather than a power failure. See The matrix → voice lanes.
first-beat.html.first-beat.006: Turn encoder 1, the leftmost knob, to the red row. This is voice 1, the factory kick drum. It has been waiting to make a fairly definite point.
first-beat.html.first-beat.008: Turn encoder 4, the rightmost knob, to move through time. Short-press it to place a note at the cursor. Put four notes on every fourth step. You now have four kicks on the floor, an arrangement of events widely considered more useful than four kicks elsewhere.
first-beat.html.first-beat.010: Short-press encoder 3. The red vertical line travelling left to right is the playhead, attending to events in their proper order. You should hear the kicks.
first-beat.html.first-beat.012: Turn encoder 1 to another voice row and add notes on steps 5, 9 and 13. The kick now has company. Whether they get along is a musical decision.
first-beat.html.first-beat.013: Give one voice the whole room.
first-beat.html.first-beat.014: Choose a voice with encoder 1, then tap touch 1, the left pad. You enter single mode, and the grid takes on that voice’s colour with the enthusiasm of a department given its own stationery. Turn encoder 1 to choose pitches and place a few notes; different rows should produce different pitches. Tap touch 1 again to return to draw mode.
first-beat.html.first-beat.016: Press encoder 3 again to stop. The beat will cease, leaving you free to investigate its accommodation: Hardware, then Matrix, then Controls.

hardware.html.hardware.001: The device, viewed as an arrangement of matter
hardware.html.hardware.002: An inventory of the ports, buttons and jacks on TŒRN. Each has a purpose, which puts them ahead of a surprising amount of matter.
hardware.html.hardware.003: A survey from a sensible altitude
hardware.html.hardware.004: The RGB LED grid occupies most of the face of TŒRN, having successfully negotiated for the best view. Four RGB-lit rotary encoders stand evenly spaced along the front strip below it. The circular capacitive pads touch 1 (left) and touch 2 (right) sit between grid and encoders; touch 3 occupies the right bottom edge. On the lower left and right edges below the matrix you will find line out, USB-C and headphones (A–C), and MIDI in, MIDI out and power (D–F). Audio and recording connections G–J run along the bottom edge, with touch 3 (K) at its right end. The letters are a map, rather than a proposed spelling of anything.
hardware.html.hardware.005: The unit from above, where its intentions are easiest to inspect. Letters identify the ports and controls in the schematic.
hardware.html.hardware.006: Line out — the sound’s departure point: 6.35 mm stereo TRS, tip left and ring right, on the lower left edge below the matrix. Connect a mixer or interface; its level is independent.
hardware.html.hardware.007: USB-C — lower left edge. Supplies power, firmware updates, serial access and USB audio output to a computer. A remarkably busy opening.
hardware.html.hardware.008: Headphone out — 6.35 mm (¼″) stereo TRS on the lower left edge. For headphones or in-ears, with adjustable level: a private audience for whatever happens next.
hardware.html.hardware.009: MIDI in (TRS) — lower right edge, Type-A TRS. Accepts standard MIDI from another device, which may have very firm views about timing.
hardware.html.hardware.010: MIDI out (TRS) — lower right edge, Type-A TRS. Sends clock and notes, allowing this device to express its own views about timing.
hardware.html.hardware.011: Power switch — a physical slide on the lower right edge. Turns the unit on and off with an unusually refreshing lack of negotiation.
hardware.html.hardware.012: Internal mic — a capsule on the bottom edge, listening for material the outside world has neglected to put on the card.
hardware.html.hardware.013: Micro SD slot — bottom edge. The residence of samples, kits, patterns and songs. Push to seat the card; push again to eject. Switch the unit off before inserting or ejecting. Moving house is best done while the landlord is asleep.
hardware.html.hardware.014: Mic in (6.35 mm) — bottom edge, between SD slot and line-in. Accepts an external microphone with adjustable gain. Its neighbour is the line-in, so a vocal mic and synth cable can remain connected without a domestic dispute.
hardware.html.hardware.015: Line in — bottom edge, 6.35 mm stereo TRS, tip left and ring right. Bring a synth, drum machine or modular system. The current recording path takes only the left input and saves mono WAVs; the right channel receives no invitation.
hardware.html.hardware.016: Touch 3 — capacitive pad on the right bottom edge, in charge of remembering noises. Use live/fast-rec from the grid, or hold it in the sample browser to enter record mode.
hardware.html.hardware.017: Things that respond to being bothered
hardware.html.hardware.018: The physical controls fall into three families, all of which expect to be consulted by the firmware:
hardware.html.hardware.019: Four RGB-lit rotary encoders, numbered 1–4 from left to right along the front edge. Turn, short-press or long-press them; their duties depend on the screen. Row 1 supplies small hints above the knobs, since remembering everybody’s job is more work than it sounds.
hardware.html.hardware.020: Three touch-sensitive pads on this hardware map: circular touch 1 (left) and touch 2 (right) between matrix and encoders, and touch 3 on the right bottom edge. Touch 1 toggles single mode; touch 2 opens the menu; both together open filters or the sample browser. Touch 3 records. For the firmware’s full touch repertoire, consult Controls → Touch pads.
hardware.html.hardware.021: Right-side power switch — physical on/off. Its vocabulary is small and decisive.
hardware.html.hardware.022: The matrix is the display. There is no additional screen or separate collection of menu buttons waiting to be discovered under a flap. The firmware conducts its entire visible conversation in lit pixels; The matrix explains the grammar.
hardware.html.hardware.024: Battery: an internal LiPo, carrying a private supply of electrical optimism.
hardware.html.hardware.025: Speaker: a small internal speaker, for giving that optimism an audible outlet.
hardware.html.hardware.026: Internal mic + Mic-in jack: a built-in microphone and a 6.35 mm external microphone input. Reality has more than one way to get a word in.

matrix.html.matrix.001: The matrix, and the difficulty of knowing where you are
matrix.html.matrix.002: Most instruments conceal their thoughts behind a screen. TŒRN has put its thoughts on the front in coloured lights, which is a much more sociable arrangement until you ask what any of them mean. The same grid displays notes, pages, menus and controls. It has no spare grid on which to explain the first one. That is why there is a handbook.
matrix.html.matrix.003: A small, unusually well-behaved piece of spacetime
matrix.html.matrix.004: Time is generally accused of going too quickly, too slowly, or somewhere you cannot follow it. Here it goes left to right, through columns 1…32, and can therefore be approached with a knob. Column 1 sounds first; column 32 sounds last. Voices occupy the other direction: upward. Row 2 carries voice 1, row 3 carries voice 2, and the arrangement continues until row 15. The apparent discrepancy is caused by row 1, which has reserved itself for helpful information. Row 16 has done the same at the top. Even a very small universe has overheads.
matrix.html.matrix.005: Coordinates, for those who would like an address: the firmware uses (x, y), counting both from 1. The bottom row is y=1; the top is y=16. “Row 1” always means the lowest visible row, however you happen to feel about the direction your life is taking.
matrix.html.matrix.006: Rows 2–15 accommodate voices. Row 1 keeps the beat guide; row 16 keeps the pages. The diagram is considerably easier to consult than a committee on numbering.
matrix.html.matrix.007: Row 1 — the reassuring business of counting to four
matrix.html.matrix.008: A musician who has lost beat one will often nod with increasing conviction in the hope that it comes back. The bottom row offers a quieter remedy. In Draw mode it shows a 4/4 beat guide: a dim marker at step 1 and every fourth step thereafter, across the grid. This row cannot hold notes. Begin placing those on row 2; the guide will remain below, being right about where the beats are.
matrix.html.matrix.009: When the cursor reaches row 16, the bottom row suspends its counting service and displays encoder hints for page-wide tools. This is intentional. A machine that can change the duties of a whole row ought at least to leave a note. The details are in Pages+More.
matrix.html.matrix.010: Row 16 — where a note editor acquires ambitions
matrix.html.matrix.011: At the top of the grid is a row of lights with a broader view of things. Each light represents a pattern page, up to 8 pages in all. This is the page strip. Put the cursor there and it becomes the TOOL-LANE: gestures that ordinarily concern one note can now concern a page. It is a short physical journey from making a mark to rearranging the landscape.
matrix.html.matrix.012:
With the cursor on row 16, you can:
  • Delete a page by unpainting its strip LED.
  • Copy and paste a page.
  • Clear the focused voice’s current edit page in single mode.
  • Generate a random, scale-aware fill for that voice in single mode.
  • Use note-shift to move that voice’s notes in time or across rows in single mode.
Row 1 shows the active tools. Move back to a voice row and individual notes become your concern again. This is how to put the landscape down before accidentally moving it.
matrix.html.matrix.013: What the page lights mean. Colour has proved more practical here than fitting a tiny explanatory plaque under every LED.
matrix.html.matrix.015: Playing and being edited: for once, what you are looking at is also what you are hearing.
matrix.html.matrix.017: Playing. Your edit cursor has gone to another page.
matrix.html.matrix.019: Being edited. Playback is on another page, or stopped.
matrix.html.matrix.021: Another page already contains notes. Something has happened here.
matrix.html.matrix.023: An empty page. Nothing has happened here yet.
matrix.html.matrix.025: Loop mode is active, and this slot is beyond the loop end. Time will turn back before reaching it.
matrix.html.matrix.026: Rows 2–15 — an incomplete census of the inhabitants
matrix.html.matrix.027: Fourteen voice lanes might reasonably lead you to expect fourteen voices. This is the sort of reasonable expectation electronic instruments find so difficult to live up to. Rows 2–15 house eight sample voices, numbered 1–8; a three-voice poly synth at 11; and mono synths at 13 and 14. Positions 9, 10 and 12 have no assigned voice. The strips at the very bottom and top are there to help you get about, and will not join in however encouragingly you look at them. In DRAW, find a voice one row above its channel number. Enter SINGLE and the vertical direction changes its meaning entirely: the rows are now different pitches of one voice. You have stayed in the same place and acquired a different sort of upstairs.
matrix.html.matrix.028: Remembering numbers is tiresome work for a creature that entered the room to fetch something and has already forgotten what. Each voice therefore has a colour. These are the standard colours, palette 0:
matrix.html.matrix.029: The eight sample voices obtain their material from the SD card; Samples explains how to change it. Voice 11 makes its own sound, with three-voice polyphony, ten presets and LFO/ARP. Voices 13 and 14 are separate mono synths with the same LFO and arpeggiator page. As for 9, 10 and 12, there really is no sound engine there. You may visit with the cursor. You may leave notes. It is rather like sending invitations to an empty house: the arrangements can be impeccable and the attendance will still be disappointing.
matrix.html.matrix.030: Readers wishing to follow a sound from its beginnings through oscillator, envelope, filter and effects should consult Sound design. Readers wishing to discover which mixer or bus it went through should consult Audio path. These are different questions, as anyone who has followed a noise through a building will appreciate.
matrix.html.matrix.031: Two things on the grid, only one of which knows the time
matrix.html.matrix.032: The first question to ask of a moving light is whether you moved it. This sorts out a surprising amount of confusion:
matrix.html.matrix.033: The edit cursor is where your next gesture will take effect. Turn encoder 4 to move it through columns, or encoder 1 to move it through rows. A row-number helper can appear beside it. The cursor has no plans of its own, which makes it a useful if rather unadventurous companion.
matrix.html.matrix.034: The playhead has plans. It is the red vertical line travelling left to right through the visible page, sounding the current column as it goes. Notes brighten when they fire. Muted lanes remain dark. Unlike the cursor, it does not wait for you to finish thinking.
matrix.html.matrix.035: Stop playback and the playhead disappears; the cursor is still yours to move. Start again and the red line resumes its journey while the cursor remains where you left it. This lets you prepare something in one place while time gets on with happening somewhere else, an arrangement people have been requesting from ordinary life for years.
matrix.html.matrix.036: Modes — the room is the same, but the furniture has changed
matrix.html.matrix.037: There is only one grid, so the device keeps finding new uses for it. The two principal ways of looking at a sequence are described in Sequencing:
matrix.html.matrix.038: Draw gives every voice full visibility. You can survey the whole arrangement, including the bits you were hoping nobody would notice.
matrix.html.matrix.039: Single brings one voice into focus and dims the others. This is helpful when a composition’s most pressing problem is that all of it is visible at once.
matrix.html.matrix.040: Elsewhere, the lights become controls or information for the task at hand. Open Menu and your sequence disappears behind text and submenu dots. The music can keep playing, which proves that losing sight of something is quite different from stopping it. To find your way through these alternative uses of the room, consult the Menu map.

controls.html.controls.001: How to make yourself understood by four knobs
controls.html.controls.002: The usual difficulty in talking to a machine is that it will do exactly what it thinks you asked. TŒRN reduces the conversation to turning, pressing and touching. This leaves very little room for a misunderstanding, and consequently makes the misunderstandings much more interesting.
controls.html.controls.003: The four encoders, none of whom has a permanent job
controls.html.controls.004: There are four knobs. Each can be turned, pressed briefly, or held for a long press. Some actions ask for two encoders held together, because a hand capable of deleting an entire page ought to bring a witness. What each knob does depends on the current screen. Where each knob is does not. Memorise their positions first; it is the one part of this arrangement that cannot be changed by opening a menu.
controls.html.controls.005: Encoder 1: “Where?” The leftmost knob usually chooses the row, voice or lane. A short press erases the note beneath the cursor in L+R draw; a long press together with encoder 4 clears the page. It is worth distinguishing the act of choosing a place from the act of removing what was there.
controls.html.controls.006: Encoder 2: “What else?” Pages, per-row volume, the mute overlay and menu values are its usual concerns. Think of it as the knob for whatever the screen considers its second most pressing problem. The screen will tell you which problem that is.
controls.html.controls.007: Encoder 3: “How does it sound?” Turning it on the grid adjusts the fast filter. A short press starts or pauses playback; menu pages give it alternate values to adjust. The same knob can make a noise more interesting or give you a moment in which to consider whether it was interesting enough.
controls.html.controls.008: Encoder 4: “When?” The rightmost knob selects columns in time and acts as the main menu navigator. Short-press to toggle grid notes or enter a menu page; long-press over an existing note for its per-step editor. This is the closest the instrument comes to asking you to be specific.
controls.html.controls.009: To avoid having to print all their changing occupations on the panel, the knobs wear RGB rings. A ring takes the voice colour on a voice lane, the page tint in filters, and white for a binary toggle. An unused knob goes dark, a form of professional honesty rarely encountered elsewhere. Row 1 repeats the colours above the encoders, so you can look from panel to grid without having to remember what you saw on the way.
controls.html.controls.010: Touch pads — easily moved, in the electrical sense
controls.html.controls.011: The firmware listens to five touch pads. Touch 1 (L) and touch 2 (R) sit between the grid and the knobs, beneath its left and right halves. Touch 3 is on the right bottom edge and records. Touch 4 auditions the current voice. Outside TOUCHY, touch 5 is FN. The first two also notice which of them you touched first, an apparently minor social detail with quite substantial consequences:
controls.html.controls.013: Enter or leave single mode. One voice becomes the subject of the conversation.
controls.html.controls.014: Enter on voices 1–8, 11, 13 or 14. Entry is blocked on row 16 and empty voice rows. Once in single, you may exit from anywhere.
controls.html.controls.016: Open the menu. The music may continue while you look something up.
controls.html.controls.017: From draw, single, paint or unpaint.
controls.html.controls.019: Open the sample browser for voices 1–8.
controls.html.controls.020: Sample voices only. A synth has no recorded file to show you.
controls.html.controls.022: Open filters for a voice that supports FX.
controls.html.controls.023: Sample or synth voices, provided the channel supports FX.
controls.html.controls.025: Go to the next filter page. The first page was only part of the argument.
controls.html.controls.028: Turn left for backward sample playback (<<), right for forward (>>). The ordinary encoder value is untouched. You are reversing the sample, rather than everything else you were doing.
controls.html.controls.029: Sample voices 1–8, outside TOUCHY and outside sample capture. In TOUCHY, touch 5 plays voice 5 instead.
controls.html.controls.031: Hold in the sample browser to enter record mode. On the grid, press/hold for live/fast-rec; see Record → Live recording.
controls.html.controls.032: In the sample browser and on the grid.
controls.html.controls.033: Holding FN changes how encoder input is interpreted. Let go and ordinary turns, clicks and long presses become ordinary again. FN plus a long press has a separate command path, but no actions are assigned to it yet. There is therefore an entire category of emphatic gestures with which you can currently achieve nothing. Experienced users of computers will find this reassuringly familiar.
controls.html.controls.034: Skin contact is enough. The pads measure capacitance, so pressing harder does not make your request more persuasive. Resting a palm on the chassis can produce an unintended touch while you turn a knob. Keep your palms clear; otherwise the machine will respond to a perfectly valid instruction you did not know you had issued.
controls.html.controls.035: Starting and stopping the local passage of time
controls.html.controls.036: A person looking for a play button will find four knobs, which may initially seem unhelpful. Short-press encoder 3 on the grid: playback starts. Repeat to stop, and the travelling playhead vanishes. Inside filter mode, use encoder 3 long press instead. This lets you hear the sound you are adjusting without leaving the editor to find out whether you have improved it.
controls.html.controls.037: Playback belongs to the whole instrument. Menus are merely something it can show you while playing. Open one to change BPM, send or receive MIDI, or load a pattern, and the loop keeps going. Imagine how much less would get done if the universe stopped every time someone opened a settings page.
controls.html.controls.038: Actions large enough to involve both hands
controls.html.controls.039: A single press is sufficient for most grid work. Some destructive actions and shortcuts require two encoders held at once. This does not guarantee that you meant to do them, but it does make an accident require more organisation. The following gestures are for draw and single mode:
controls.html.controls.040: Page-row tools require the cursor on row 16 (y==16). Delete page, copy/paste, randomize, single-mode clear and note-shift belong to the page strip. Before repeating an unsuccessful gesture with mounting conviction, inspect the “Where” column. The correct gesture in the wrong place is still the wrong instruction.
controls.html.controls.042: Delete the page beneath the cursor by unpainting its strip LED. The page’s notes are cleared.
controls.html.controls.045: Clear the focused voice on the current edit page. Other voices keep their notes.
controls.html.controls.048: Generate a random, scale-aware fill for the focused voice. It is possible to delegate inspiration; results vary.
controls.html.controls.051: Enter note-shift to move the focused voice’s notes.
controls.html.controls.054: Open mute/solo while held; release to return. Encoder 3 adjusts fast filter, encoder 4 chooses a random sample.
controls.html.controls.057: Open the focused voice’s filters. You can now change the sound without first finding another one.
controls.html.controls.060: Toggle the note at the cursor. It will either begin to exist or stop doing so.
controls.html.controls.063: Open the per-step note editor for the existing note. Even a very brief sound can turn out to have a complicated personal history.
controls.html.controls.066: Clear the page: all voices in draw, only the focused voice in single. “All” is doing important work in this sentence.
controls.html.controls.069: Jump to BPM, where tempo, clock source and brightness are settled. Loudness has its own arrangements under VOL.
controls.html.controls.071: For a two-encoder action, hold both within the long-press window. The order in which you release them does not matter. The relevant chapters spell out the pairing: “long-press encoder 1 together with encoder 4,” for example. Trying to perform this as a dazzling feat of finger speed makes it considerably harder to do as a simple thing with two hands.

troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.001: When reality fails to follow the instructions
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.002: Sooner or later the machine will do something unexpected. This is a normal stage in the relationship between a person and an object with firmware. Before either of you does anything permanent, consult the complaints below. Resets come afterwards, where it becomes particularly important to read past the reassuring name.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.003: A catalogue of quite specific disappointments
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.004: Half the matrix is dark. Has the other half resigned?
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.005: The firmware believes it is addressing a different quantity of LED boards. Being firmware, it has expressed this belief with complete confidence. Open ETC → ADV → LEDS and try 1, 1B, 2 and 2B in turn until the geometry agrees with the actual hardware. The B variants flip the image for boards mounted upside down. This is an orientation setting, rather than a judgement on the person who mounted them.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.006: The headphones are presenting a very convincing performance of silence.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.007: Silence can be introduced at several points, and the headphones have no means of telling you which one is responsible. Work through VOL → MAIN (above 0), VOL → GAIN (1.0x is the old mix staging; 0.0x mutes a bus), and VOL → SPKR (check whether speaker routing is taking over). Seat the headphone plug fully. If line-out works but headphones still do not, inspect the TRS jack for a hardware fault. At this point the silence has become a physical matter.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.008: The samples exist, but the browser does not believe in them.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.009: The browser remembers its file list. This saves time until you change the files, when it saves a somewhat less useful version of time. Run ETC → RSET → SD to rescan without disturbing patterns. If the files remain absent, check that they are 16-bit mono WAV at 44.1 kHz and that the card follows the layout in the SD card chapter. A correct filename is encouraging, but insufficient evidence of a correct file.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.010: The SD tool cannot find a serial port to speak to.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.011: Use desktop Chrome or Edge at sdtool.tyng.app. Android and Pixel browsers usually cannot see the Teensy USB serial port, however prominently it exists. On the device, keep ETC → SD open; WAIT becomes OK when connected. Opening the port can reboot the Teensy, which is an unusually dramatic way to answer the telephone. If it leaves that page, reopen ETC → SD after Connect. See SD card → SD tool.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.012: Both machines agree on the beat, but disagree on the exact instant of it.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.013: Two kicks separated by a few milliseconds are sufficient to make synchronisation sound like a philosophical dispute. Open MIDI → SYNC: SNC1 delays the outgoing path and SNC2 the incoming one. Loop back a metronome and adjust in ±2 ms steps until both kicks land together. Leave the page to save the setting. Agreement, in this case, is measurable.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.014: The BPM number is red and appears nervous.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.015: The device is on EXT clock, waiting for timing from outside. That timing is unstable or missing. Check the master’s cable and clock settings, or use BPM → encoder 3 to select INT and let TŒRN keep its own time. Outsourcing the passage of time only works if the contractor turns up.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.016: I changed kits and my perfectly good pattern became something else.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.017: The notes still point at the same voice rows. Those rows now contain different samples. It is rather like giving the same set of stage directions to a different cast, particularly if one of the actors is a cymbal. Select the old KIT number and short-press encoder 1 on the KIT screen to reload it. For future productions, save a PATT per KIT and write down the matching KIT number.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.018: I cleared the wrong page. I would like the previous universe back.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.019: There is no undo in RAM. Reload a previously saved PATT slot if you have one. Without a saved copy, the cleared work cannot be recovered. This is the point at which a handbook is often expected to produce a secret key combination. It has none. Save to PATT whenever an idea becomes worth regretting.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.020: The battery percentage has a relaxed relationship with truth.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.021: The number is an estimate from the charger IC, rather than a tiny observer counting electrons as they leave. Treat it as a fuel gauge, not laboratory equipment. Before trusting its curve, give it at least one complete cycle: charge over USB until full, then run until shutdown. Precision improves when the gauge has met both ends of the journey.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.022: The touch pads are receiving instructions from someone else. There is no one else.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.023: Check where your palms are. Capacitive pads detect skin contact, including contact made by portions of you that were not planning to operate the instrument. Lift your grip clear of the pads. If the problem persists in dry conditions, power-cycle the unit to recalibrate the baseline. The supernatural explanation can usually be postponed until after this step.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.024: A slow turn of an encoder produces a surprisingly adventurous value.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.025: The I²C encoders can occasionally lose synchronisation. Power-cycle the unit. Occasionally, reseating the SD card also helps; switch the unit off before doing so. If the jumping persists, investigate a hardware fault. Continuing to turn more carefully is unlikely to cure a knob that has ceased to agree with arithmetic.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.026: A long press on encoder 4 gives me painting when I wanted note detail.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.027: A long press is capable of meaning more than one thing, which is precisely the sort of economy that makes manuals necessary. Check the current SETT → DRAW setting: in L+R, encoder 4 also handles held painting. Release any active paint gesture and check the editor instructions in Note detail. To move from draw to single mode first, tap touch 1 on a valid voice. Repeating the same press harder does not add a footnote explaining your intentions.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.028: Something is moving on the grid without my permission.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.029: If it is a bright dot with a short trail bouncing through your pattern in draw mode, check whether MODE → PONG is ON. That is PONG. It strikes and fires notes on muted voices only; ordinary unmuted playback is left alone. Turn it off on the same page, or adjust its speed with encoder 2, 1–99. If, after prolonged inactivity while stopped, you see two cartoon eyes, that is the separate idle animation. The machine is looking back at you. It has not acquired an opinion; it has acquired something to do while you acquire one.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.030: Both touch pads were touched. The sample browser remained unimpressed.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.031: The sample browser requires a sample voice, 1–8, and the left pad first. A synth row leads to the filter editor instead, because there is no sample file there to browse. Turn encoder 1 to a sample row and try the combination again. Simultaneity, in the world of touch pads, is often a matter of who got there first.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.032: I left note-shift and cannot find the notes where I expected them.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.033: Note-shift saves continuously and commits the positions when you exit with encoder 4 short press. Check neighbouring pages: a nudge may have moved a note beyond the part of the pattern you can currently see. This is a location problem that can look remarkably like a memory problem, especially to the person who moved the thing.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.034: The sample preview would like the entire room’s attention.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.035: Lower VOL → PREV. For fewer unsolicited performances, change VOL → PREV from ON to PRSS, then press encoder 1 to audition. Or use SYNC to hear the file on the voice’s pattern hits. You can then consider a sample before allowing it to announce itself to everyone else.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.036: ETC → RSET: six ways to make things simpler
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.037: Reset is an appealing word. It suggests that everything will become like new, and neglects to mention how little of your work existed when everything was new. Encoder 3 selects the reset mode; encoder 4 confirms it. Read the effects and survivors below before pressing. The six options do substantially different things.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.042: Rescan the whole card, write samples/toern_wavs.txt for mute-mode random preview ?>, and invalidate the sample-browser cache. SCAN, a green checkmark, then back to draw: the catalogue has caught up with the shelves.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.043: Everything except the stale browsing/random index. Use after a card-reader swap or SD tool transfers.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.045: Return filters, envelopes, synth parameters, octave helpers and audio effects to factory values across every voice. The tone controls forget everything you taught them.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.046: Patterns and sample assignments survive. All tone settings return to factory values.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.048: Clear all notes, velocities and probabilities; set BPM to 100; reset volumes and filter data; delete and rewrite autosaved.txt; rescan the card. “FULL” is not a modest claim.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.049: The panel setting under ETC → ADV → LEDS (1 / 1B / 2 / 2B) and PATT-saved patterns survive. Almost nothing else in RAM does.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.051: Delete the saved pattern files 1–999.txt. This removes the copies you might otherwise have reloaded.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.052: autosaved.txt and the current session in RAM survive.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.054: Delete kit folders except KIT 1. The exception is worth reading twice.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.057: Delete autosaved.txt, its .tmp and .bak recovery files, and clear the grid.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.058: Settings, PATT slots and kits survive. Unless you pause-autosave again, the next boot is blank. If the session itself is damaged, use FULL instead.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.059: There is no undo beyond reloading saved pattern files. FULL destroys unsaved work in RAM. This warning is deliberately short, in the hope that it arrives before your finger does.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.060: If it still refuses to be a musical instrument
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.061: Soft restart: switch off, wait five seconds, switch on. Most freezes end here. Five seconds is a long time to a processor and an agreeably short time to everyone else.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.062: Reseat the SD card: power off, push to eject, reinsert firmly, then power on. This resolves many missing-sample problems that survive a rescan. The card must actually be in the slot, rather than merely optimistic about its position.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.063: Reflash the firmware: use USB-C and the Teensy 4.1 boot procedure. A firmware reflash leaves pattern files on the card alone unless you also reformat the card. Those are two separate operations; do not let their proximity in a troubleshooting session introduce them to each other.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.064: Persistent touch problems: make the chassis clean and dry, then reboot. Capacitive baselines are recalibrated at startup. Allow the instrument to form its first impression without a palm on its face.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.065: For a failed encoder, dead LED or scratchy jack, inspect the hardware. The schematic and KiCad sources are in PCB/toern_revG/. Software has many faults, but it cannot mend a broken connection by becoming more thoughtfully configured.
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.066: You may now return to the interesting noises
troubleshooting.html.troubleshooting.067: If the machine has resumed behaving, this is a good moment to make music before either of you thinks of something else to investigate. If a display remains mysterious, the Screen index will take you to its explanation. And save to PATT before switching off: a very small administrative act which prevents a surprisingly large amount of philosophy.

sequencing.html.sequencing.001: Sequencing, or arranging for things to happen again
sequencing.html.sequencing.002: A sequencer is a machine for remembering when a noise should happen, so you can devote your attention to whether it ought to. Here are draw, single, and the L+R and R methods of placing or removing triggers. Page-wide affairs live in Pages+More; mutes, note-shift, copy/paste and random generation have expanded into Advanced Sequencing.
sequencing.html.sequencing.003: Draw mode — the universe as you left it
sequencing.html.sequencing.004: After startup you arrive in draw mode. Every voice is visible at full intensity, the red playhead crosses all the rows together, and the cursor marks the place you are about to change. This gives you an overview of the entire arrangement. Whether an overview makes you feel in control depends chiefly on the arrangement.
sequencing.html.sequencing.005: Four voices have left notes on this page. The playhead is behind column 7, on its way to finding out what they meant by them.
sequencing.html.sequencing.007: Choose the voice lane under the cursor. Its colour identifies the voice, rather than your current degree of certainty.
sequencing.html.sequencing.009: Remove the note under the cursor. The lane remains unmuted; encoder 2 handles muting. Erasing an event and asking someone to be quiet are quite different interventions.
sequencing.html.sequencing.011: Hold and turn to erase a trail. A long press together with encoder 4 clears the whole page across all voices. Check the scope before applying the enthusiasm.
sequencing.html.sequencing.013: Under SETT → CTRL, PAGE makes this knob change pattern pages; VOL makes it adjust the current row’s volume. A knob can only do so much until someone tells it what kind of knob it is today.
sequencing.html.sequencing.015: Mute or unmute the current voice. Its notes remain in place, prepared for a change of heart. See Advanced → Mutes.
sequencing.html.sequencing.017: Hold to solo the current voice; while held, encoder 3 adjusts fast filter and encoder 4 chooses a random sample. Release to return. See Advanced → Mutes.
sequencing.html.sequencing.019: Adjust the parameter assigned as default on this channel’s filter page. This is the shortcut to the particular thing you decided you would want a shortcut to.
sequencing.html.sequencing.021: Start or pause the sequencer. Time agrees to wait for another press.
sequencing.html.sequencing.023: Open the focused voice’s filter editor, provided its channel supports FX. You can investigate the sound more thoroughly there.
sequencing.html.sequencing.025: Move the cursor through steps 1…32. This is time travel on a deliberately restricted budget.
sequencing.html.sequencing.027: Place a note at the cursor if the cell is empty. The future now contains an appointment.
sequencing.html.sequencing.029: On an empty cell, hold and turn to paint a trail. On an existing note, open the per-step editor. Establish whether there is already a note there before attempting to improve the emptiness.
sequencing.html.sequencing.030: Single mode — the benefits of a smaller problem
sequencing.html.sequencing.031: There comes a point in arranging music when the helpful thing is to stop looking at most of it. Single mode brings the selected voice to full intensity and lets the others fade to their base colours. The editing logic remains familiar, but one instrument can now be considered without the rest of the composition waving at you.
sequencing.html.sequencing.032: The focused voice is bright white; its neighbours retain dim base colours. They have not been deleted. They have been asked to wait.
sequencing.html.sequencing.033: From draw, select voice 1–8, 11, 13 or 14 and tap L (touch 1) to enter single mode. Tap again to return. You cannot enter from row 16 or empty voices 9, 10 and 12; first choose a voice that exists. Once inside, row 16 remains available for page tools. Draw gestures still apply, but copy/paste takes only the focused channel, the encoder 1 + encoder 4 long clear-page chord clears only that channel, and page-row randomize fills only that channel. This is the advantage of narrowing your attention: your mistakes acquire a smaller geographical range.
sequencing.html.sequencing.034: On causing a note to exist, and subsequently regretting it
sequencing.html.sequencing.035: A lit step is a trigger: an instruction to play this voice at this point in time. It is a tiny prediction which the sequencer is obliged to make come true. Placing one is called paint; clearing one is unpaint. Your method depends on SETT → DRAW, where the instrument asks how many hands you would like involved in these decisions.
sequencing.html.sequencing.036: L+R or R — a question of available hands
sequencing.html.sequencing.037: L+R and R use the same grid and store the same notes. They disagree only about which knob should be responsible for their existence. In L+R, writing and erasing belong to separate encoders. In R, encoder 4 does both, while encoder 1 discovers a talent for dramatic silence.
sequencing.html.sequencing.039: Two hands: left on encoder 1, right on encoder 4.
sequencing.html.sequencing.040: One hand, doing most of its work on encoder 4.
sequencing.html.sequencing.042: Short-press encoder 4; hold and turn to paint a trail.
sequencing.html.sequencing.043: Short-press encoder 4 on an empty cell; hold and turn to paint.
sequencing.html.sequencing.045: Short-press encoder 1; hold and turn to erase a trail.
sequencing.html.sequencing.046: Short-press encoder 4 on a lit cell; hold and turn to erase.
sequencing.html.sequencing.048: Turn encoder 1 to choose the voice.
sequencing.html.sequencing.049: Still encoder 1. Some familiar landmarks survive.
sequencing.html.sequencing.051: Erase the note. A small, local absence.
sequencing.html.sequencing.052: Temporary full mute for a performance break. A much larger absence, with a return journey.
sequencing.html.sequencing.054: Careful editing, with the voice in one hand and time in the other.
sequencing.html.sequencing.055: Live drawing with one hand, plus quick performance breaks.
sequencing.html.sequencing.056: Change this under SETT → DRAW whenever you like. The pattern does not change. Only the means by which your hands can interfere with it are revised.
sequencing.html.sequencing.057: L+R paint — dividing creation between two hands
sequencing.html.sequencing.058: Your left hand chooses who. Your right hand chooses when, then presses to make it happen. If all collaborations divided their responsibilities this clearly, bands would require fewer vans.
sequencing.html.sequencing.059: Turn encoder 1 to select another voice row. This changes who gets the next note.
sequencing.html.sequencing.060: Turn encoder 4 to choose a step in time. This changes when they get it.
sequencing.html.sequencing.061: Tap encoder 4 to place a trigger at the cursor. The arrangement has acquired an event.
sequencing.html.sequencing.062: Hold encoder 4 and turn to leave a continuous trail of triggers. A brisk way of making the near future rather busy.
sequencing.html.sequencing.063: L+R: encoder 1 chooses the voice lane; encoder 4 moves through time and writes. Both hands can plausibly claim to have composed the beat.
sequencing.html.sequencing.064: L+R unpaint — the left hand edits the right hand’s optimism
sequencing.html.sequencing.065: Encoder 1 is the eraser. It can therefore undo the right hand’s placement of a note without entering into a lengthy discussion about why the note seemed such a good idea a moment ago.
sequencing.html.sequencing.066: Tap encoder 1 to remove the trigger under the cursor.
sequencing.html.sequencing.067: Hold encoder 1 and turn to erase a trail. An extended passage can become an extended pause with very little effort.
sequencing.html.sequencing.068: In L+R, writing stays on encoder 4 and erasing stays on encoder 1. One knob does not toggle between them. You always know whether the hand in question is adding to the composition or developing a more critical attitude towards it.
sequencing.html.sequencing.069: R mode — creation and destruction on the same knob
sequencing.html.sequencing.070: Select DRAW = R and encoder 4 takes both jobs. Tap an empty cell to place a trigger; tap a lit cell to remove it. Hold and turn for a trail: the state of the starting cell decides whether the whole gesture paints or erases. The knob makes that decision when you press, then sticks to it. This is useful consistency, provided you looked at the starting cell.
sequencing.html.sequencing.071: Tap encoder 4 to toggle the cell: empty becomes trigger, trigger becomes empty.
sequencing.html.sequencing.072: Hold encoder 4 and turn: start on empty to keep painting, or on a trigger to keep erasing. The first cell sets the policy for the journey.
sequencing.html.sequencing.073: Turn encoder 1 to choose the voice row. It has relinquished erasing, rather than all responsibility.
sequencing.html.sequencing.074: R mode: encoder 4 places and removes triggers. Encoder 1 is available for a rather theatrical interruption.
sequencing.html.sequencing.075: The performance break — making everybody notice the next noise
sequencing.html.sequencing.076: With erasing moved to encoder 4, a press of encoder 1 becomes a temporary full mute. Everything falls silent. This is a performance break, and can make the return of a perfectly ordinary kick drum seem like the arrival of an important person. Which encoder you press to leave the mute decides who returns:
sequencing.html.sequencing.077: Encoder 1 again: restore the mute states you had before. Resume the previous arrangement of people speaking and people wisely keeping quiet.
sequencing.html.sequencing.078: Encoder 2: unmute only channels 1 and 2. A comparatively intimate comeback.
sequencing.html.sequencing.079: Encoder 3: apply your custom return set from SETT → MUTE. Rehearsal can be advantageous even for a surprise.
sequencing.html.sequencing.080: Encoder 4: unmute everything. Subtlety has had its turn.
sequencing.html.sequencing.081: SETT → MUTE defines that custom set of voices to bring back. It does not restrict which rows you may paint. For example, prepare a “kick and snare only” return and a single press can bring those two out of the silence, while the rest remain quietly impressed by the restraint.
sequencing.html.sequencing.082: For a whole-page removal, go to the page row and, in L+R, unpaint its strip LED with encoder 1; see Pages+More → Delete a page. Alternatively use the encoder 1 + encoder 4 long chord, or single-mode clear, on the current edit page. A performance break keeps the notes. Clearing a page removes them. Both produce less music, but only one is expecting it back.

pages-more.html.pages-more.001: A short history of wanting another page
pages-more.html.pages-more.002: At first, one page is an enormous amount of space. You can put a kick here, a snare there, and still have room for several errors of judgement. Then you write something you like. Immediately it becomes necessary to have a second page in which almost the same thing happens, but with a slightly different hi-hat. This innocent requirement is how arrangements begin. Row 16 provides the extra territory and the means of moving, copying and clearing it. The more elaborate consequences are discussed in Advanced Sequencing.
pages-more.html.pages-more.004: Move encoder 1 to the very top, row 16 (y==16). The dots are your 8 pattern pages. Each looks reassuringly small. This is misleading: a page dot represents a whole stretch of music, much as a modest dot on a map can represent a town containing a station, three supermarkets and somebody who is absolutely certain you have parked in their space. From here, your gestures operate on that larger thing.
pages-more.html.pages-more.005: The cursor must be on row 16. That is the condition for delete page, copy/paste, clear, random fill and note-shift. On a voice row (y ≠ 16), the same buttons paint, erase, mute or do nothing. This is worth checking before pressing the button several more times. Increasing the frequency of a wrong instruction has never made a computer understand the right one, though it has kept generations of computer owners very busy.
pages-more.html.pages-more.006: The bottom hints and encoder rings change colour when the cursor reaches the page row. Think of this as the instrument looking up from its desk and saying, “A whole page? Are we doing whole pages now?” Ordinary draw/single colours mean that it has not yet been informed of the expansion.
pages-more.html.pages-more.007: Having reached the top, you may now make the following substantially larger decisions:
pages-more.html.pages-more.008: Delete a page by unpainting its strip LED. This removes notes, rather than merely making the little light less obtrusive.
pages-more.html.pages-more.009: Copy and paste the page. Draw takes all voices; single takes the focused voice. The hi-hat variation that started this whole business is now within reach.
pages-more.html.pages-more.010: Clear the current edit page for the focused voice: single mode, encoder 1 short press.
pages-more.html.pages-more.012: Note-shift moves the focused voice in time or across rows, in single mode. It is the instrument’s answer to the very human conviction that the notes would be excellent if only they were somewhere else.
pages-more.html.pages-more.014: The page LEDs report occupancy using hasNotes. They can tell you whether something is there. They cannot tell you whether it ought to be there. This limitation has proved beneficial to relations between the instrument and its owner.
pages-more.html.pages-more.021: The demolition of a very small dot
pages-more.html.pages-more.022: There is a moment in almost every creative project when its author decides that one section is beyond saving. Occasionally this is sound judgement. Occasionally the author needs lunch. The instrument cannot distinguish these conditions. On the page row, unpaint clears the entire page beneath the cursor. A dark-blue occupied page becomes empty, and the machine assumes that this was what you meant.
pages-more.html.pages-more.023: Put the cursor on row 16. Check the changed hint colours. You are about to act on a page, so it is useful to be on one.
pages-more.html.pages-more.024: With encoder 4, choose the page LED you intend to clear. Dark blue means it has notes. Consider them briefly.
pages-more.html.pages-more.025: In DRAW = L+R, press encoder 1 on that strip LED. This is the operative part of the decision; everything before it was merely looking determined.
pages-more.html.pages-more.027: In draw, all voices across that page’s 32 steps are cleared. Every instrument on the page receives the same short notice.
pages-more.html.pages-more.028: In single, only the focused voice is cleared. Other voices remain, and the page stays occupied until all of them are empty. A bassline cannot declare a page vacant while a perfectly serviceable snare is still living there.
pages-more.html.pages-more.029: A fully empty page turns very dark red. The playback range, lastPage, also updates, removing trailing empty pages from the journey. The machine is therefore prepared to stop visiting a place once you have removed everything worth visiting. Many transport authorities could learn from this.
pages-more.html.pages-more.030: R mode has a different arrangement. Encoder 4 on the page strip performs copy/paste. For strip erasing, use L+R or the clear-page gestures below. Copying a passage you were trying to remove is an especially efficient way to discover how much you disliked it.
pages-more.html.pages-more.031: There is no undo. Save the page to PATT before clearing it if you might want it back. The future has a habit of becoming rather sentimental about things the present found intolerable.
pages-more.html.pages-more.032: Check which page “clear” means. Strip unpaint at y==16 targets the LED under the cursor. Encoder 1 short in single mode on the page row targets the focused voice on the current edit page. The encoder 1 + encoder 4 long chord also targets the current edit page, from any row: all voices in draw, focused voice in single. Two different pages may be involved. They are not obliged to be the same merely because you have been thinking of them both as “the page.”
pages-more.html.pages-more.034: Row 1 has four cues, one above each encoder, repeated by the rings. They are a compact substitute for having a tiny person beside each knob explain its present responsibilities. The tiny people were considered impractical, and would almost certainly have formed opinions about the music.
pages-more.html.pages-more.056: On the page row in draw, encoder 1 is red and encoder 4 yellow. Page dots continue to show content, and the cursor marks the target. These lights remain admirably factual during moments when the musician’s intentions have become largely emotional.
pages-more.html.pages-more.057: Red over encoder 1, yellow over encoder 4. You have the larger tools out.
pages-more.html.pages-more.061: L+R unpaint clears all voices on the page under the cursor. The strip LED becomes dark red when empty.
pages-more.html.pages-more.063: Clear every voice on the current edit page, which may differ from the cursor’s page LED. No undo; check the destination before demolishing it.
pages-more.html.pages-more.071: In single mode, open the focused voice’s filters. In draw, the page row maps to channel 15, which has no filter path. There is nothing there to make warmer.
pages-more.html.pages-more.073: Move across steps and pages; the edit page follows the cursor’s position. You are choosing where the next operation will land.
pages-more.html.pages-more.075: First tap: copy the current edit page, all voices. Second tap: paste onto the page you have reached. See Advanced → Copy & paste. Music can now repeat without requiring you to repeat yourself.
pages-more.html.pages-more.077: The first encoder 4 tap darkens the page strip and produces large blue encoder 1 and large yellow encoder 4 hints. A copy is now in the buffer. Nothing visible resembles a parcel, which is why it is easy to forget you are carrying one until it arrives somewhere surprising. Continue with Advanced Sequencing → Copy & paste.
pages-more.html.pages-more.078: Single, with room for one more good idea
pages-more.html.pages-more.079: Single uses red, white and yellow hints on encoders 1, 2 and 4. The copy contains only the focused voice. You can copy the hi-hat, change focus, and paste onto a different voice. The new voice receives the rhythm without receiving any explanation of why the hi-hat thought it appropriate. This is, in miniature, how musical traditions spread.
pages-more.html.pages-more.080: Single’s red, white and yellow hints. The rest of the band is safe from this particular experiment.
pages-more.html.pages-more.082: Clear every note of the focused voice on the current edit page. No undo. The other voices are outside this particular decision.
pages-more.html.pages-more.084: Generate a fresh scale-aware pattern for the focused voice on this page. See Advanced → Random. The machine is willing to suggest an alternative; it cannot guarantee you will prefer it.
pages-more.html.pages-more.094: First tap copies the focused voice; second tap pastes onto the voice currently in focus. See Advanced → Copy & paste.
pages-more.html.pages-more.095: Clear and randomize cannot be undone. The last PATT save is your way back. If the page was never saved, the handbook can offer sympathy, but it would be dishonest of it to describe sympathy as a recovery procedure.

advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.001: Some experiments in making the music behave differently
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.002: A groove is a small community of noises that have reached a temporary understanding. Advanced sequencing lets you test the understanding. You can silence one member, move another, duplicate the entire gathering, or invite a machine to suggest what is missing. The community may improve. It may also become so interesting that you reload the old pattern. Page-row geography is in Pages+More; the ordinary means of making notes are in Sequencing.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.004: Most of these tools require row 16, y==16, usually in single mode. Mutes need a voice row. Row 1 indicates which tool is armed; consult Pages+More for the colours. A naturalist searching for a particular creature begins by finding its habitat. The same principle applies to note-shift, although note-shift is considerably less likely to bite.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.006: One of the quickest ways to improve a piece of music is to stop part of it. This is an awkward discovery, and musicians have developed elaborate vocabulary to avoid making it sound personal. On a voice row, hold encoder 2 for the temporary mute/solo overlay. The other lanes mute, leaving the current voice alone. Release to restore them. A short press toggles the lane’s mute persistently. Nothing is erased. The noises have been asked to wait outside, rather than informed that the species is extinct.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.007: Muted lanes dim. Active lanes remain bright. The silence is represented without requiring a blank display.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.008: While encoder 2 is held, you can examine the surviving voice more closely:
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.009: Encoder 3, green: the current voice’s fast filter. An isolated sound can now be persuaded to become less obviously the reason you isolated it.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.010: Encoder 4, pink: browse the random sample playlist, ?> / ?<, and short-press to load the last preview. This is rather like asking whether the drummer could improve the groove and being offered a waterfall. Try it before dismissing it.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.012: On row 16, encoder 2 short enters note-shift in single mode. To mute, return to a voice row. The machinery distinguishes the removal of a sound from the relocation of its notes even when its operator is still deciding.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.013: R mode’s temporary full mute is a separate arrangement on encoder 1. Its return options are in Sequencing → R mode and SETT → MUTE. There are surprisingly many varieties of silence. Most become distinguishable at the moment they end.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.015: Imagine discovering that an animal’s entire migratory route was one step too far to the left. A large research grant would be needed to move the landscape. Note-shift is cheaper: it moves actual step data through time and across rows. Moving rows is the grid’s transpose operation; there is no separate global transpose page. If you want to change the pitch while leaving the written steps alone, use detune and octave in Sound design. This distinction matters chiefly when you later look for the notes where you left them.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.016: In single mode on row 16, short-press the white encoder 2. Other voices are snapshotted while the focused one becomes movable. Encoder 1 glows bright green, encoder 4 bright blue, and a grey marquee crosses row 1. It is a reassuring quantity of visible preparation for what can otherwise look alarmingly like the notes deciding to leave.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.018: Shift the focused voice vertically across the whole pattern. Notes wrap at the edges. The world is round in this rather specialised direction.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.027: The white page-row cue is the sign for note-shift. Encoder 2 short on a voice row will not enter it. Check the habitat before concluding the creature has disappeared.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.029: On the page row, short-press encoder 4 to copy. Draw takes all voices on the edit page; single takes only the focused voice and can paste it into another voice after a focus change. An exact repetition may be described as structure or as a lack of ideas. The machine wisely leaves that decision to the reviews.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.031: The first tap stores the copy, darkens the page strip and shows large blue encoder 1 and large yellow encoder 4 hints. Navigate to the destination, then tap encoder 4 again to paste. Another tap while armed without pasting toggles the armed state off. This is a useful moment to remember whether you wanted the phrase here, there, or merely somewhere that would make it easier to think about.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.032: Blue and yellow, with the page strip dark: a copy is ready. The original has survived the journey so far.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.034: First tap: fill the buffer. Second tap: paste onto the current page and, in single, the current voice. Confirm where you are before making there more like here.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.036: Single mode, row 16, red encoder 1 cue: long-press encoder 1. This is in-grid randomize. On a voice row, the same long press may erase a trail. The distinction is particularly worth checking when your plan is to let the machine contribute, since deleting your contribution first can give it an exaggerated sense of its importance.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.037: The companion replaces only the focused voice on the current edit page. It studies the other voices across the active pattern, giving the current and neighbouring pages extra weight, and responds to accents, velocities and tonal centre. In other words, it listens before joining in. This is such a promising innovation in musical collaboration that one is tempted to make it compulsory. It assumes the following roles for the channels:
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.041: Kick and snare retain rhythmic anchors, though the snare may arrive a step early or late in response to kick, clap and ensemble density. Hats, claps and toms explore sparse Euclidean patterns with different pulse counts and full 16-step rotations; claps can reinforce a snare or fill a vacant backbeat. On 32-step pages the second half gets a related rotation. Every role may use different pitch rows. Bass responds to kick, existing bass and harmony, preferring root and fifth. Bass, keys and pads share a page-level key, scale and four-slot progression, such as minor i–VI–III–VII. Sample keys and pads stay monophonic; synth lanes 13 and 14 take one tone each of a two-note chord. Channels 1–8 never receive stacked chords. Channel 11 permits three voices, though its bass role normally writes one note. Choices weight approximately 60% chord tones, 30% other scale tones and 10% chromatic passing notes. That last ten per cent is where a computer briefly looks as though it has had an interesting childhood. Faster tempos thin the decorations. With no other voices to study, it invents a varied 4/4 starting point. Long-press again for another reading of the evidence.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.042: Clear and randomize have no undo. Recover from the last PATT save. The companion will listen, suggest and try again, but remains entirely incapable of remembering the particular unsaved version you have just decided was perfect.
advanced-sequencing.html.advanced-sequencing.043: For a larger experiment, use MODE → AUTO. It studies the orange base-page range and writes coordinated variations into the following green pages. An empty base creates a complete starter ensemble. The astonishing thing is less that it can develop your ideas than that it will make this effort even when you have supplied no ideas at all.

samples.html.samples.002: There are sounds which people travel great distances to hear, and sounds which cause people to move house. A sampler is admirably free of prejudice about the distinction. Both become data. The sample browser is where you find a recorded noise, trim its less promising extremities, and decide whether it deserves one of voices 1–8.
samples.html.samples.004: Before entering the undergrowth, settle the size of the expedition. KIT replaces the samples for all eight voices, as explained in Sample kits. SMP changes one current voice, channel 1–8, using a file under samples/. SMP provides trim, reverse, preview and load. It is entirely possible to spend an agreeable evening selecting a single snare. The instrument imposes no upper limit on this activity, and cannot be held responsible for what happens to the evening.
samples.html.samples.005: The noise must be a mono 16-bit WAV at 44.1 kHz, at most 12 seconds per voice. These conditions apply regardless of the sound’s rarity, emotional significance or resemblance to a dying refrigerator. The SD card chapter explains how to get it aboard.
samples.html.samples.007: Select sample voice 1–8 and open SMP, or touch both pads left first from draw, single or menu. Four large row-1 letters announce the available equipment: P, magenta, for preview; Y for trim end; G for load; W for browser. Beneath them is a waveform. It is the first hint that the enormous alarming sound in the headphones consists largely of something that looks like a disappointed caterpillar.
samples.html.samples.009: Turn encoder 4. The combined list begins with [../], then subfolders, then .wav files inside the current directory under samples/. A good folder system is invaluable here. So is remembering which good folder system you were using when you named the files.
samples.html.samples.010: A WAV displays peaks and waveform between its trim boundaries. At least you can now see the sound you cannot quite describe.
samples.html.samples.011: A folder or [../] displays breadcrumbs on row 6: green dot for root, yellow chevrons, then a letter per folder segment. This will get you home, provided home is somewhere under samples.
samples.html.samples.012: A file selected: waveform and the trim bar on y=3. The specimen has been sighted.
samples.html.samples.013: A folder selected: the path replaces the peaks. You are looking at where noises live, rather than at a noise.
samples.html.samples.017: On a file, go up one directory. At the samples root, do nothing. This intentional refusal saves a surprising amount of exploratory wandering.
samples.html.samples.019: Very few recorded events start exactly when they become interesting. There is usually a click, an intake of breath, and somebody saying “Is it on?” Trim lets you reject these preliminaries without claiming they never happened. Positions run from 0–100% of the decoded file.
samples.html.samples.020: Turn encoder 1 to move the start. It stops before the trim end. The instrument insists that even a very short sample should contain some time.
samples.html.samples.021: Turn encoder 2 to move the end. It stops after the start. Creation of a sample whose ending precedes its beginning has been left to a more expensive product.
samples.html.samples.022: Row 3 shows a dim blue baseline. Green lies before the trim start; red lies after the end. The illuminated interval is what remains to be played. A surprising number of excellent samples are discovered by removing most of an apparently unpromising one.
samples.html.samples.024: Press encoder 1, short or long, to audition the WAV in ON or PRSS, or in SYNC while stopped. It stays in the folder. During running SYNC, this press does not play the file; the pattern is already asking the questions.
samples.html.samples.025: Encoder 2 short reverses the sample, flips its picture and restarts preview. A familiar sound heard backwards often turns out to have been concealing an entirely different sound. Press again to turn it back. This is considerably easier than persuading the original event to repeat itself in reverse.
samples.html.samples.026: Under VOL → PREV, ON makes each selection audition immediately; PRSS waits for encoder 1. SYNC auditions automatically while stopped and, during play, substitutes the highlighted file on this voice’s pattern hits. SYNC is particularly useful when every sample sounds excellent on its own and most of them sound dreadful in the actual song. The song is allowed to attend the interview.
samples.html.samples.028: Short-press encoder 3 to load the selected file and autosave the pattern. Trim and reverse become part of this voice’s sample until another file is loaded. Turning encoder 3 has no assigned function. It is the expedition member who carries nothing until the moment it becomes absolutely necessary to carry the specimen.
samples.html.samples.029: For a sound which has not yet been captured, hold touch 3 to enter Record. Exercise some care: once you begin hearing the world as sample material, perfectly ordinary household objects start to look under-employed.
samples.html.samples.034: Audition the selected WAV in ON/PRSS, or SYNC while stopped. Remain in the folder; listening is not a navigational act.

sound.html.sound.002: It is possible to spend forty minutes turning a perfectly good sound into a perfectly good sound. The two sounds are different, which provides compelling evidence that the forty minutes have been well spent. Whether the second is better is a more delicate question, usually settled by making a third. Sound design offers envelopes, filters, delay and effects, with reverb on selected voices, to assist this investigation. It is an absorbing occupation. Keep an occasional version of the sound you began with, if only to discover why you were so enthusiastic about improving it.
sound.html.sound.003: What happens after a note happens
sound.html.sound.004: Follow a sample through the chain below. It acquires a shape, loses some information, has parts of its spectrum discouraged, and may be sent into an artificial room. Reverb is available on voices 1, 2 and 5–8 and the poly synth; voices 3, 4, 13 and 14 have no send. A sound can undergo a great deal of improvement before reaching the listener. Occasionally it survives the improvement completely unrecognisable, at which point people say it has character.
sound.html.sound.005: The diagram is a useful account of the musical journey. The actual route through Teensy mixers, gains and buses is documented in Audio path. Bitcrush sits before the SVF. A filter given a crushed signal is doing a different job from a crusher given a filtered signal, rather as a cleaner working before a demolition team is having a different afternoon from one arriving afterwards.
sound.html.sound.007: From the grid, touch both pads right first. Left-first on sample voices opens the sample browser, which solves the problem by finding another sound altogether. The filter editor gives each page four vertical encoder columns. Turn to change a value; short-press a column to make it the voice’s fast-filter default, recalled with encoder 3 in draw. Encoder 2 long toggles play/pause here, and touch 2 cycles pages. You now have the means to change the sound while repeatedly hearing what you have done. Try to regard the latter as evidence.
sound.html.sound.008: The letters become words when disturbed. At rest each slider has one letter, because the matrix has accepted a four-column layout without first securing room for a dictionary. Turn a knob and the lower rows spell its four-letter parameter name in the matching colour. Stop and the small letter returns. A control can consequently spend most of its life looking cryptic while becoming quite explicit at the precise moment you no longer have a spare hand to point at it.
sound.html.sound.009: Page 0: the sample makes its first alterations
sound.html.sound.011: Resting labels: H · L · R · B. The sound is under four kinds of supervision.
sound.html.sound.013: Turning LCUT makes LCUT appear in full. The instrument has briefly abandoned abbreviation.
sound.html.sound.020: Low cut uses the SVF highpass. At 0, HCUT’s lowpass path is used; values 1–32 switch to highpass. Choose which end of the spectrum is causing the trouble.
sound.html.sound.030: Reverb routing is a physical limitation of the audio graph. Voices 1, 2, 5–8 and 11 have RVRB. Voices 3 and 4 show an inactive dim slider; mono synths 13 and 14 replace the third control with CENT, coarse pitch, on page 0. There is a peculiar temptation to keep adjusting an unavailable effect in case it suddenly becomes available. The author can report that this occupies time very successfully.
sound.html.sound.031: Page 1: resonance, pitch, and a small disagreement with duration
sound.html.sound.033: Voices 1–8 show R · D · O · T: four letters behind which a sample can undergo considerable personal change.
sound.html.sound.035: Encoder 4 is moving, so the display spells TIME. This is unusually explicit behaviour from time.
sound.html.sound.050: WSOLA changes duration independently of the playback-rate pitch change provided by OCTV. The sample can take longer to finish without having to explain itself in a correspondingly deeper voice.
sound.html.sound.051: Range 0–22. 11 is OFF, the default. Below 11 shortens by roughly −10%…0%; above 11 lengthens by roughly 0%…+10%.
sound.html.sound.052: OCTV/DTNE alter playback rate and pitch. TIME alters duration around the current pitch. Keep TIME at 11 for OFF. Move it when the stretching and its associated smear are part of the intention. There is an important stage in learning any instrument at which one discovers that a control can be left at its default for reasons other than cowardice.
sound.html.sound.053: An echo takes the long way back
sound.html.sound.054: On sample voices 1–8, the fourth page has one DLAY slider. This is a real delay tap, AudioEffectDelayExternal in PSRAM. 0 is off; N is N/32 of a beat. Values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 give even divisions, and the intervening values give intervening arrivals. At 32 the delay is one beat and follows BPM, rather than being fixed at 1.2 seconds. Feedback recirculates the tap while dry sound stays present. Synth voices 11, 13 and 14 put the same control on CRF, encoder 4. An echo is a fascinating collaborator: it contributes nothing new, insists on having another turn, and can transform the entire piece if you let it speak at the right moment.
sound.html.sound.057: Voices 11, 13 and 14 share C · R · F · D. Their agreements extend to the layout, rather than necessarily to the sound.
sound.html.sound.059: Turning encoder 2 spells RESO. The resonance is requesting attention.
sound.html.sound.062: Voice 11 uses the poly ladder for cutoff. Voices 13/14 use the SVF tied to HCUT. The knobs have similar names because musicians would otherwise have to learn the plumbing before making a tune.
sound.html.sound.076: Page 2: choosing a temperament for the oscillator
sound.html.sound.078: The resting letters are W · I · C · S. A brief address for the oscillator’s identity and tuning.
sound.html.sound.080: Turning encoder 2 spells INST, making the instrument selection less of a guessing exercise.
sound.html.sound.083: Change oscillator 1. Uniform three-oscillator presets change all three together. Selecting INST restores and displays the preset’s waveform default. A preset arrives with a past; the first waveform edit is where your relationship with that past begins.
sound.html.sound.097: ADSR, or how a noise conducts itself in public
sound.html.sound.099: A · D · S · R: attack, decay, sustain, release. Four stages in a sound’s relationship with being audible.
sound.html.sound.101: Moving encoder 3 spells SUST. You are adjusting the part that stays.
sound.html.sound.102: A note being told to start is a surprisingly incomplete instruction. Should it arrive like a slammed door or like someone remembering why they entered the room? Attack sets the journey from trigger to peak. Decay takes it from the peak to the sustain level, which remains while the note is on. Release governs its departure after note-off. Each encoder spans 0–32, mapped to milliseconds for A/D/R and 0–1.0 for sustain. The four values describe a sound’s manners so comprehensively that one begins to wonder why they are not fitted to people.
sound.html.sound.103: Leave release until last. A long release allows notes to spill into the next step. A short one with high sustain gives a firm, staccato drum. Much can be achieved by teaching a sound when to leave, particularly if it has been occupying the room with an account of its own importance.
sound.html.sound.104: A closer look at the envelope
sound.html.sound.105: The envelope-generator design is shared by all voices. Channel 11 adds a separate filter ADSR controlling cutoff. Reach it through voice 11’s filter page 1; the third filter row swaps in for filter-ADSR where applicable.
