Its four controls look familiar, but now the envelope changes what frequencies get through rather than simply how loudly the sound arrives. Similar shapes can conceal quite different intentions. A rising hill, a rising bill and a rising filter cutoff are best distinguished before attempting to climb any of them.
sound.html.sound.108: Release 0 shuts the note at the next step. A busy groove sometimes improves when its inhabitants stop leaving their coats over the next person’s chair.
sound.html.sound.120: Reverb uses a shared global bus. Supported voices send to it through RVRB; page 0 shows which they are. Think about the room you are implying. A tiny drum can become a ceremony in a cavern, and eight sounds in the same cavern can become an extremely expensive way of hearing very little clearly. Balance the sends against dry signal, allowing the sound to retain enough of its original outline to be found again.
sound.html.sound.121: A useful thing within immediate reach
sound.html.sound.122: You will probably discover one control that you keep returning to, rather as a person in a strange kitchen eventually discovers the location of the kettle. Give it a shortcut. In the filter editor, short-press its column to choose the voice’s fast-filter default. Back in draw or single, turn encoder 3 to adjust it. What was a journey through pages becomes a reflex, leaving more of your attention available for whatever the tune is trying to do.
sound.html.sound.123: The shortcut remains available on encoder 3 while encoder 2 holds the mute/solo overlay. Its ring is green; random samples move to encoder 4 during the hold. The sound can be examined alone without putting the kettle back in another cupboard.
sound.html.sound.124: HCUT is a useful sample default and CUT a useful synth default. Each channel remembers its own choice. Uniformity is overrated in a collection containing both a kick drum and a noise you obtained by hitting a saucepan.
sound.html.sound.126: Voice 11 and the possibility of three notes at once
sound.html.sound.127: A monophonic instrument solves many problems by refusing to play a chord. Voice 11 takes the more adventurous approach: three voices of polyphony, with three oscillators per voice. Its ten presets are BASS · KEYS · CHPT · PAD · WOW · ORG · FLT · LEAD · ARP · BRSS. Each combines waveforms, envelope shape and filter-envelope amount. Independent amplitude and filter envelopes, pan, gain, waveform, cents and semitones offer considerable scope to improve things, followed by considerable scope to wonder which improvement caused the present difficulty.
sound.html.sound.128: An instrument selection installs matching register, filter, waveform and ADSR defaults. PAD and WOW swell; ORG has clean drawbar harmonics; FLT is breathy; LEAD a square-forward pluck; ARP a tight pulse stack; BRSS a darker saw body whose filter blooms more slowly. Listen to the attack and departure as well as the sustained note. That is where much of the apparent personality lives. Edit the defaults freely; saved projects retain the edits, including the ones you made while trying to hear what the unedited preset sounded like.
sound.html.sound.129: The fifth page matches voices 13/14: LFO R · LFO D · SPAN · ARP. The LFO moves cutoff and resonance in the shared SVF and poly ladders. ARP acts only on MIDI-held notes; it leaves notes already on the grid as written. This last restraint is welcome in a machine that has otherwise been given several opportunities to develop a tune’s personality without consulting its author.
sound.html.sound.131: Voices 13 and 14 each have two oscillators and a full ADSR. They are monophonic. Page 0’s third column is CENT, coarse pitch, in place of RVRB; these voices have no reverb send. Their two performance modulators are quite enough to keep one note occupied:
sound.html.sound.132: LFO: rate 0.25–10 Hz, with 0 off; depth 0–100%. Full depth sweeps cutoff ±6 octaves and also modulates resonance. It runs independently of SPAN/ARP. A low-frequency oscillator is a machine for returning to the same opinion regularly, a quality widely admired in filters and rather less in dinner guests.
sound.html.sound.133: ARP: MIDI hold only. Centre 16 is off. Above it gives sixteenths; below it eighths. Distance sets the interval amount. Grid notes retain their written pitches. In SINGLE while playing, each arp hit records at the pitch actually sounded. A quick experiment with a held note can therefore leave a much more elaborate account of itself than you remember performing.
sound.html.sound.134: Available shapes include sine, sawtooth, square and triangle. Basslines and leads often need only one note at a time. Polyphony is an excellent facility to possess, but it should not be allowed to become a moral obligation.
sound.html.sound.135: Ordinary notes restart the envelope. For a continuous phrase on synth 11, 13 or 14, mark the destination note G/L in note detail. The same pitch holds the existing envelope; a different pitch retunes the active voice without restarting it. Without an adjacent source, G/L attacks normally; a gap ends the phrase. Every other note already retriggers, so no separate R/T setting is needed. The difference is audible: a series of separate arrivals can become one creature moving through the room.
sound.html.sound.137: Voices 9, 10 and 12 have no sound engine. You can take the cursor there and place notes, but no audio path will answer. See The matrix → voice lanes. The emptiness is deliberate. It would be unwise to spend an entire evening adjusting its filter, though the resulting silence might possess a very consistent tonal quality.
sound.html.sound.138: How far from the original note?
sound.html.sound.139: Global transpose is a semitone offset in the synth path, currently a code-level hook initialised to 0. No menu page exposes it. This description is provided chiefly to save determined people an expedition through menus in search of a setting that has not been given a door.
sound.html.sound.144: The offsets add together. Detune and octave handle the broad placement; cents and semitones refine it. If the result is unexpectedly far from the starting pitch, retrace the additions before suspecting a new and revolutionary tuning system.
sound.html.sound.146: There may come a point at which you have adjusted a sound so extensively that nobody, including the sound, remembers what was wrong with it to begin with. In the channel’s filter editor, encoder 4 long resets its envelopes, filters and synth data while leaving the notes intact. To reset the sound layer for every voice, use ETC → RSET → EFX. One returns a specimen to its original condition; the other tidies the whole collection.
sound.html.sound.147: EFX reset affects all 16 channels. Patterns and sample assignments survive; filter, envelope, synth and octave-helper settings return to defaults. Save a sound worth keeping before deciding that a fresh start would be refreshing.

audiopath.html.audiopath.001: The case of the travelling noise
audiopath.html.audiopath.002: A noise enters the instrument, acquires a filter, visits a mixer and eventually appears in the headphones. This sounds straightforward in much the same way that “take a train to the coast” sounds straightforward before the replacement bus service is mentioned. Here is the complete route through Teensy Audio objects to the SGTL5000, with mixer input numbers and actual programmed gains. The relevant timetables are audioinit.h, toern.ino, toern_filter.ino and toern_synths.ino.
audiopath.html.audiopath.003: The fixed points of the investigation
audiopath.html.audiopath.034: An unwritten AudioMixer4 gain defaults to 1.0. Only explicitly assigned gains appear in firmware. In ordinary life, failing to give someone an instruction often leads to nothing happening. A mixer input left without this particular instruction passes everything at unity. It is worth learning which sort of absence you are dealing with.
audiopath.html.audiopath.036: There is one lane per channel. Bitcrush comes before the state-variable filter. Voices 3 and 4 have no reverb object and go directly from filter mixer to mixer1. They will arrive with no account of the room that the other samples visited. They did not go there.
audiopath.html.audiopath.067: The addresses at mixer1 are: input 0, channel 1’s reverb mix; input 1, channel 2’s reverb mix; input 2, channel 3’s dry filter; input 3, channel 4’s dry filter. mixer2 inputs 0–3 carry channels 5–8’s reverb mixes. Keep this list when tracing an unexpected sound. Guessing which bus contains it by how bus-like it sounds is seldom productive.
audiopath.html.audiopath.069: Voice 11 begins with three oscillators for each of three voices. It splits through left/right pan mixers, then collapses to mono for shared bitcrush, filter and reverb processing. The old waveform11_1/2 objects remain in existence but are muted at gain 0 so they cannot enter reverb while stopped. They are the passengers whose tickets have been cancelled but who remain visible on the platform, causing occasional concern to people reading the diagram.
audiopath.html.audiopath.081: Voices 13 and 14 put two oscillators through a mixer and one envelope acting as VCA. They have no reverb, and page 0 displays CENT in its place. There is less luggage to account for, though the oscillators are still quite capable of making a considerable scene.
audiopath.html.audiopath.135: Three hot sample hits in one bank bring its mixer to approximately 1.0 at GAIN 1.0x/1.0x. Both banks enter mixer_end at 0.50 + 0.50 = 1.0 before synth at 0.60 and monitor are added. VOL → GAIN scales 1–4, 5–8, SYN and ALL from 0.0x to 2.0x; 1.0x matches these tables. Four full-level hits on one bank can clip. Lower a GAIN control, or use MIX_BUS_HEADROOM at 0.25 if the pattern requires four. It is tempting to reason that four individually excellent sounds must add up to an even better sound. A fixed-point mixer has a distressingly literal objection to this argument.
audiopath.html.audiopath.136: peakOutput watches mixer_end for the LED-strip meter. It changes nothing. The fact that the meter has seen a disaster does not confer on it the ability to prevent one.
audiopath.html.audiopath.137: A sample appears for an audition
audiopath.html.audiopath.138: VOL → PREV maps 0–50 to gain 0–0.5. The RAM path is 25% hotter to match SD; MAIN, LOUT and channelVol are independent. If the preview appears to have travelled outside the normal voice controls, that is because it has.
audiopath.html.audiopath.139: The entrance, the recording, and the temptation to listen
audiopath.html.audiopath.149: The codec selects MIC or LINEIN with inputSelect. micGain is 0–63, or 0 for line. lineInLevel is 0–15. Before tracing a missing signal halfway across the graph, check that it was permitted through the entrance.
audiopath.html.audiopath.151: VOL → 2-CH writes mixer_stereoL/R. Hardware right is I2S DAC 0, left DAC 1. There is nothing intrinsically wrong with this numbering. The difficulty begins only when someone assumes that numbering must somehow make left and right more obvious.
audiopath.html.audiopath.173: L+R takes mixer1, voices 1–4, to the left and mixer2, voices 5–8, to the right. It mutes mixer_end on both sides, removing synths 11/13/14 and input monitoring from that mode. Stereo input 3 stays 0. VOL → GAIN bank trims and ALL still work on mixer1/2; SYN has no effect in L+R. A missing synth here has followed the routing perfectly. It has merely followed it to somewhere you are not listening.
audiopath.html.audiopath.183: Persons mentioned in the diagram but absent from the performance
audiopath.html.audiopath.186: envelope11 is patched into mixer_waveform11 input 2, whose gain is held at 0. The active poly envelopes are Senvelope1/2. The diagram records a connection; the gain records whether anybody uses it.
audiopath.html.audiopath.187: The two output mixers also feed usb1, so USB audio carries the same two-channel routing as headphone and line outputs. The computer hears the mix that leaves by those doors, without receiving a private improved edition.
audiopath.html.audiopath.188: When investigating clipping: count four simultaneous sample hits on a bank; inspect voice 11’s reverb stacked on dry at 0.72 + 0.72; consider BITC plus RVRB, since crush precedes the tanks. Muting releases envelopes so tails do not accumulate. Finding the offending sum is less glamorous than discovering a mysterious defect in a sample, but has the considerable advantage of allowing you to fix it.

record.html.record.002: A recording expedition begins with the reasonable belief that a world making so much noise ought to contain something worth bringing home. It frequently ends with an excellent recording of the bag in which the microphone was kept. Between these events, a bird may have called, a door may have produced an extraordinary creak, and somebody will almost certainly have asked whether you were recording. TŒRN can capture sound onto sample voices through its dialog or live grid recording. REC sets input, gain, trigger and clear policy. Set them before the interesting noise. The interesting noise has not read this chapter and cannot be expected to wait.
record.html.record.003: Preparation, before the interesting bit happens
record.html.record.004: In the sample browser, hold touch 3 to record into the current sample voice. The file is written into the current browse folder with a number such as rec_01.wav. Set the folder first. Discovering a wonderful take three weeks later among files labelled for a different experiment can be delightful, but is not a dependable filing method.
record.html.record.005: To keep the whole output on a computer, connect USB-C with a data cable, select TŒRN’s USB audio device in your DAW or recorder, and capture both channels. The routing follows VOL → 2-CH, like headphone and line out. This records the output directly and creates no sample on the SD card. Before searching for the take, recall which machine you asked to remember it. Several computers connected by a cable do not constitute one large, cooperative memory.
record.html.record.006: Threshold, live level, RDY and Y/R/G/X hints. The recorder is ready. The world is under no obligation to produce something worth recording.
record.html.record.017: A threshold-armed take stops after about one second below half the threshold. Maximum length is 12 seconds per voice. Input, gains and clear policy are in the REC submenu. Twelve seconds will comfortably hold many remarkable events. If your event needs an introductory lecture, record the event and consider whether the lecture could be supplied separately.
record.html.record.018: Recording while something else is happening
record.html.record.019: The eight-channel live-loop flow lets you hold touch during playback and capture up to twelve seconds onto a voice. One-shot recording can place a take onto a single channel. This is useful when the sound belongs to the performance itself and would be greatly inconvenienced by an application form and a pause in proceedings.
record.html.record.020: REC → TRIG controls the beginning; REC → CLR controls the fate of previous notes. The normal grid entry is touch 3; see Controls → Touch pads. Choose these policies in a quiet moment. During the exciting moment, your hands will be busy and your judgement may be occupied by how exciting the moment is.
record.html.record.021: Five small questions asked in advance
record.html.record.022: The root family REC contains input, microphone gain, line trim, trigger and note-clear policy, navigated with encoder 4. People often think the important part of recording is the red button. Experienced people tend to spend much of their time checking the cable attached to the thing that comes before it.
record.html.record.023: REC at the root menu. You have reached the part of the expedition concerned with bringing evidence home.
record.html.record.024: Where the sound is coming from
record.html.record.028: The stereo TRS line jack accepts synths, drum machines and modular gear. Recording uses the left input only and saves mono WAVs. If the right side contains the entire performance, its absence from the file will be entirely explicable.
record.html.record.029: Input selection determines which gain matters: MIC or L-IN. Turning the wrong one is soothing, but does little for the recording.
record.html.record.030: The microphone needs a little assistance
record.html.record.033: The line input needs rather less
record.html.record.035: Line-level equipment is already loud, so L-IN adjustment is coarser than MIC. Synths are often happy around 6–10. Their owner may be happier with a larger number, but the recorded signal has the better-informed opinion.
record.html.record.040: Hold touch 3 to capture immediately; release to stop. Default. Suitable for an event whose schedule has not been discussed with the recorder.
record.html.record.042: Hold touch 3 for a dotted-red three-second countdown: 3–2–1. Capture begins at 0 and continues until release. Let go early to cancel. These are three useful seconds in which to clear your throat, reconsider the microphone position, or remember what noise you were about to make.
record.html.record.045: What happens to the old arrangement?
record.html.record.046: A new sample can inherit the old voice’s notes. It may find them congenial. It may be a long, delicate noise inheriting an arrangement originally written for a snare, in which case the relationship can become difficult almost immediately. CLR decides whether those notes survive the replacement.
record.html.record.056: Clear the notes and add a trigger on step 1. The new sample has been given one uncomplicated opportunity to say what it is.

note-detail.html.note-detail.001: A note is asked some further questions
note-detail.html.note-detail.002: From a distance, a note is a light. Come closer and it turns out to have velocity, probability, conditions and a relationship with the volume of its entire voice. This is generally what happens when you examine anything closely enough. Long-press encoder 4 over an existing note to begin the examination.
note-detail.html.note-detail.004: In draw or single, place a note, then long-press encoder 4 on it. The grid is replaced by four vertical value bars and small labels. The note still sounds as playback reaches it, so it can demonstrate the consequences of your enquiries. This is more informative than asking whether a velocity of eighty-three feels right in the abstract.
note-detail.html.note-detail.005: Red-orange velocity at left; five probability stops; a fraction such as “1/2”; blue-cyan voice volume at right. It is the sort of portrait in which the sitter discovers it has been looking complicated all along.
note-detail.html.note-detail.006: Turn the encoders to adjust their bars. Long-press encoder 1 to leave. Changes are already active in RAM; use PATT to save them. A note can be permanently altered in memory while remaining completely unrecorded on the card, a distinction of interest chiefly to people who are about to switch off.
note-detail.html.note-detail.007: Read the scope before turning velocity. In SINGLE, it edits this note. In DRAW, it edits every note assigned to the voice across all pages. Probability and condition affect only this note; voice volume affects the whole voice. It is possible to enter this editor intending to have a quiet word with one note and accidentally address the entire population. The machine will assume that was a stylistic choice.
note-detail.html.note-detail.008: Four approaches to the same small occurrence
note-detail.html.note-detail.009: Medium velocity, an uncertain probability, condition “1/2,” high voice volume. The note is quite prepared to be heard, on the occasions when it is prepared to be there.
note-detail.html.note-detail.011: Velocity 1–127. SINGLE changes this cell; DRAW changes all notes of this voice across all pages. A small turn can therefore have a large audience.
note-detail.html.note-detail.015: Choose 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% or 100%. Each playback visit may skip the step accordingly. A note at 0% remains a remarkably detailed proposal for an event that will never occur.
note-detail.html.note-detail.021: Humans routinely agree to do something on every other occasion, then devote substantial effort to deciding whether the present occasion counts. The condition column removes the argument. Its fractions specify when a step fires as the pattern reaches it, with additional settings for ratchets and glide. The machine keeps the count. You are free to find the resulting occasional noise spontaneous.
note-detail.html.note-detail.041: Glide/legato into this destination note on synth voices 11, 13 and 14. The destination determines how the previous note is allowed to become this one.
note-detail.html.note-detail.042: The same pitch holds the envelope; another pitch slides without restarting it. Without an adjacent source note, attack normally. Samples treat G/L as 1/1. A sample has a recorded past of its own and cannot simply be persuaded to acquire the synth’s continuous present.
note-detail.html.note-detail.043: Probability and condition both apply. A 50% note set to 1/4 waits for the appropriate fourth visit and then tosses a coin. On the other visits it does not even toss the coin. If you are trying to establish whether such a note is broken, allow time for it to be merely behaving exactly as requested.
note-detail.html.note-detail.044: Observations made while waiting for the note
note-detail.html.note-detail.045: The envelope still matters. With a long attack, low velocity may never establish itself before the next step. Adjust attack alongside velocity; see Sound → ADSR. Making a shy entrance quieter does not generally help it get noticed.
note-detail.html.note-detail.046: Try 75% on the hi-hats. The pattern loses some of its certainty without acquiring additional written notes. Listen over several loops. The musical effect is the changing pattern of omissions, which cannot be properly appreciated by hearing the first pass and immediately deciding it is wrong.
note-detail.html.note-detail.047: A 4/1 ratchet plays four hits in a step. Lower velocity or lane volume to compensate. A quiet sound repeated four times may be interesting. A loud sound repeated four times is often a very effective way of drawing attention to the volume control.
note-detail.html.note-detail.048: This screen edits one step. For a shared row velocity, use the velocity encoder live during playback in single with SETT → CTRL = VOL. It is worth choosing whether your concern is the individual or the whole row before beginning a prolonged series of private conversations.

files.html.files.001: The idea which existed until you switched off
files.html.files.002: There are two great pleasures in electronic music: finding that a series of quite unreasonable sounds has become something wonderful, and finding it again the next morning. The second is less celebrated, perhaps because there is seldom an audience for a successful file operation. PATT supplies that pleasure. This chapter covers numbered saves, loading, NEW, stored settings, autosave, and the samples kept separately in kits.
files.html.files.003: A numbered place in the future
files.html.files.004: Open PATT from the root menu. Each slot is one numbered file on the card, preserving all pages, voice lanes, per-step values and tone settings. Sample audio is stored separately. Think of a pattern as everything needed to tell the musicians what to do, rather than an improbably small cupboard containing the musicians. This distinction becomes painfully clear when an excellently preserved rhythm is played by eight entirely different samples.
files.html.files.005: The occupied slot shows a large green number and green load icon. Something is there. Whether it is the thing you fondly remember remains to be established.
files.html.files.007: Load the file into RAM and make it the live pattern immediately. The number brightens green while loading, reflecting whether the file exists. A dim-blue empty slot opens NEW. Asked for a pattern that has never been saved, the instrument offers to invent one, which is generous, but should not be mistaken for miraculous recovery.
files.html.files.009: Save into the chosen slot, overwriting its existing file. There is no second confirmation. The instrument takes a deliberately pressed save button as sufficient evidence of a deliberate decision. In this respect it has a rather high opinion of us.
files.html.files.011: Encoder 3 controls whether loaded sound settings are applied to the live audio objects. The settings are inside the pattern file; the details below explain exactly how much restraint this switch provides.
files.html.files.013: Slot 0, marked A, loads session recovery and cannot be saved manually. Slots 1–999 store numbered patterns. The colour reports existence, which is the first and least demanding test of a file.
files.html.files.016: Green is occupied, blue empty. A green animated checkmark confirms a successful save; a red animated cross reports failure. Wait for the result. A button press is an intention. The checkmark is what the card has to say about it.
files.html.files.017: The invention of a previously nonexistent past
files.html.files.018: The first PATT entry is NEW. Select it and press encoder 1; an empty dim-blue slot also takes you there. The generator uses the same scale-aware engine as single-mode randomize and places the result in RAM. It is particularly useful on days when you are quite prepared to make music but have discovered that the music has made no corresponding preparations to be made.
files.html.files.019: Cyan NEW title; a genre selected; a pink length bar unless BLNK is chosen. The machine is asking what kind of beginning you would like.
files.html.files.023: Choose 1–16 pages for a genre. BLNK disables the length control and its bar. The blank option contains no hidden starter pattern. It is an unusually honest use of the word blank.
files.html.files.025: Available labels are BLNK, TECH, HIPH, DNB, HOUS and AMBT. Four letters allow a surprising amount of musical intention, though not much room for an explanation of how genres relate to one another.
files.html.files.027: Run the generator and return to the grid with the new pattern live. Take a moment to listen before deciding which of its apparent mistakes you wish you had thought of.
files.html.files.028: The same genre and length can produce different results on every run. Save a keeper with PATT before asking for another. A random generator is very good at generating the next thing, and completely indifferent to your sudden realisation that the previous thing had something.
files.html.files.029: NEW replaces the current RAM pattern. A genre template may also adjust BPM and related state. Save before using it if the current idea matters. This is one of the few cases in which making a fresh start can erase the evidence that you had already started rather well.
files.html.files.030: The contents of a deceptively named file
files.html.files.031: A pattern is a binary file in the SD root, with a name such as 42.txt. It contains all pages, step values, sound settings, mutes and the 64-slot arrangement. There is no separate .dat or sidecar. The extension is misleading: opening the file as ordinary text will not reveal a pleasantly written account of the bassline. It will reveal binary data, which is a perfectly good way of storing a bassline and a very poor way of discussing one.
files.html.files.032: Turning encoder 3 OFF stops loaded filter, envelope and synth settings being applied to the live audio objects. The stored settings are still read into memory. It is neither a notes-only import nor a way to retain a separate copy of your present sound settings. A switch labelled with a small concept can affect a smaller part of an operation than the mind is inclined to infer. Read this distinction before attempting an ingenious recovery technique that depends on it not existing.
files.html.files.033: Sample audio is outside the pattern. Keep its matching kit and custom samples on the card. A saved pattern may remember exactly when the crash cymbal entered while possessing no cymbal with which to make the entrance.
files.html.files.034: The machine makes some notes of its own
files.html.files.035: Pause playback, or successfully load a sample, and the firmware requests a save to autosaved.txt. Successful autosaves have a five-second cooldown; closely spaced actions may not produce separate checkpoints. Numbered PATT slots remain untouched. Autosave is rather like a conscientious travelling companion who occasionally writes down where you are. It is enormously better than having no such companion, but you should still put an address on the things you particularly want to keep.
files.html.files.036: Startup loads recovery. Each save uses a temporary file belonging to its destination, such as autosaved.txt.tmp or 42.txt.tmp, and preserves the previous generation as .bak. A valid destination takes priority. If it is missing or unreadable, a complete temporary or backup file for that destination may be recovered. The old shared pattern.tmp is not loaded automatically because it does not identify its target. Somewhere in this apparent fussiness is the very desirable principle that recovering one tune should not quietly become replacing another.
files.html.files.037: ETC → RSET → ASAV deletes recovery and its transaction files. FULL resets the session and writes empty recovery. Saving an empty grid to a numbered slot deliberately clears that slot, its temporary file and backup. Autosave still preserves an empty session. The machine respects the possibility that you wanted nothing. It has no reliable way to tell that possibility apart from the nothing you are about to describe in rather strong language.
files.html.files.038: Save important work to a numbered PATT before switching off. The physical switch does not perform a shutdown save. Anything after the latest checkpoint is lost if power disappears. Electricity has proved a remarkably cooperative medium for making music, but has never agreed to remain available because you are nearly finished.
files.html.files.039: Remembering the band as well as the tune
files.html.files.040: PATT saves notes and sound settings. KIT saves the sample audio for voices 1–8. Save both after recording or replacing samples if you want to reconstruct the session. Loading a pattern does not reload its samples. The composition can survive perfectly while its entire acoustic world has changed, a possibility that is either artistically exciting or the start of a very long evening.
files.html.files.041: For recall, load the matching KIT, then the PATT with sound-setting application enabled. To remix, load a different kit before the pattern. Keep a record of the kit number beside the pattern number. The version of yourself who returns after a week will be a capable, intelligent person with absolutely no knowledge of why you considered these two numbers memorable.

sd-card.html.sd-card.001: A small geography of stored things
sd-card.html.sd-card.002: The supplied card is already prepared. This is worth enjoying for a moment. Much human effort has been spent inventing storage devices and then discovering that they must first be prepared, formatted, populated, mounted, persuaded or spoken to by a different computer. For the present, put the supplied card in the category of problems somebody has already dealt with. What follows is for the day you wish to change it.
sd-card.html.sd-card.003: Two routes to the same collection
sd-card.html.sd-card.004: To alter the card, use the SD tool while it remains in TŒRN, or connect it to a computer with a card reader. The contents reached by both routes are the same. Only the number of very small objects you must handle before reaching them differs.
sd-card.html.sd-card.005: The card stays where it is
sd-card.html.sd-card.006: Open Menu → ETC → SD and leave it open. The file server runs only on that page; the display reads WAIT, then OK when connected. In desktop Chrome or Edge, visit https://sdtool.tyng.app, press Connect and choose the Teensy serial port. You can browse, upload, download, rename or delete. Uploaded WAVs are converted to 44.1 kHz mono 16-bit. Drop several files, a whole folder with its subfolders, or a .zip, extracted in the browser into the current SD folder. This is a civilised arrangement: the card remains in the instrument, and the carpet is denied another opportunity to become the permanent custodian of expensive miniature electronics.
sd-card.html.sd-card.007: Remain on ETC → SD throughout. Opening the serial port can reboot the Teensy. If it leaves the page, reopen ETC → SD after Connect. Desktop browsers are required; Android/Pixel Chrome usually cannot see this USB serial port. After substantial transfers, use ETC → RSET → SD if the browser list is stale. Do this before concluding that the computer has eaten your files. It may merely be describing an earlier and, from its point of view, perfectly satisfactory arrangement of them.
sd-card.html.sd-card.009: If you need the original contents, open the TŒRN Sample converter at audioconvert.tyng.app. Under SD CARD, download SD-CARD-CONTENT.zip. Extract it and copy every file and folder to the card’s root, rather than into a new enclosing folder. The full instructions are there. File systems have an innocent-looking ability to contain a perfectly complete copy of the right thing one level too deep to be any use. The distinction is small enough to miss and large enough to occupy the rest of the afternoon.
sd-card.html.sd-card.010: If the new contents do not appear after boot or SD-tool use, run ETC → RSET → SD. The rescan asks the instrument to reconsider the actual card instead of continuing to explain what it remembers. This is sound advice for people too, though regrettably they have no corresponding menu item.

sample-packs.html.sample-packs.001: The same notes, inhabited by different noises
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.002: A remarkable amount of a pattern’s identity resides in the sounds that happen to be playing it. Replace the samples and a sensible drum part can become a conversation between objects that have never previously met. A KIT changes all eight sample voices together. This chapter explains that operation, its relationship to PATT, and the provisional wilderness called kit 0.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.004: There are up to 999 numbered kit folders, 1–999, on the card. Each supplies the audio for voices 1–8. Loading another kit replaces all eight samples while leaving the pattern untouched. If you doubt how much meaning depends on context, try a rhythm written for acoustic drums with a kit consisting largely of things that squeak. Every event will arrive exactly on time. This will not necessarily make the events seem reasonable.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.005: Kits fill sample voices 1–8. Synth voices 11, 13 and 14 generate their own sound and remain unchanged. Voices 9, 10 and 12 have no assignment. The operation is comprehensive within its jurisdiction, a phrase the three empty voices might have found reassuring if they had any means of hearing it.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.007: Open KIT at the root. It resembles PATT: number, load icon, save icon. The similarity is convenient until one forgets that a pattern and its samples are different things. Keep the distinction in mind, especially when pressing a save icon with the cheerful belief that everything has now been taken care of.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.008: KIT: a familiar screen containing a different kind of memory.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.010: Load eight WAVs from the highlighted folder into RAM, replacing the sample voices. Brightness indicates whether the folder is populated. The pattern continues to issue its old instructions, apparently unaware that everyone receiving them has changed.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.012: Write the current eight samples into the selected numbered folder, replacing its files. Wait for the green animated checkmark; a red cross means the kit was not fully saved. The computer’s reply matters more than how convincingly you pressed the button.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.016: Choose a numbered kit. Green folders exist; blue folders are missing. Kit 0 is the automatic scratchpad, where the samples you are currently thinking about tend to accumulate.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.019: Switching kits replaces all eight sample voices. Save to PATT first if you need recall. A new kit is a new interpretation, and does not preserve the old interpretation merely by sounding completely different from it.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.020: The place where temporary things become important
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.021: Load a single sample through the sample browser and the mapping is written automatically into KIT 0, surviving reboot without an explicit save. Treat it as a scratchpad. This is where you put a sample just to try it, then another, then a third, until the entirely provisional collection becomes the most interesting thing you have made all week. The scratchpad will not realise that its status has changed. You must tell it.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.022: Choose a numbered KIT slot and press encoder 2 to save the present eight samples there. You have now promoted the collection from something you were doing to something you can deliberately come back to.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.024: Kit numbers correspond to numbered folders on the microSD. The starter layout in the SD card chapter contains the following, with a commendable lack of imaginative names:
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.025: 0/, 1/ … 999/ hold the WAVs for voices 1–8 and optional extras. A directory called 27 may contain your favourite set of noises in the world. Its name will make no attempt to communicate this.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.026: Files such as 1.txt and 2.txt at the card root are binary patterns and their settings. They contain what the sounds should do, rather than the sounds themselves.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.028: The firmware indexes the card at boot. After swapping cards, offline changes or SD-tool transfers, run ETC → RSET → SD if the list looks stale. Indexes are excellent at remembering. They require occasional assistance in discovering that the thing they remember has changed.
sample-packs.html.sample-packs.029: The starter card uses a loose geography: lower kit numbers for acoustic drums, middle numbers for house/techno, higher for synth-only kits. Continue it if useful. A working convention saves you from the much more personal geography in which every important thing is located “somewhere around where I put it last time.”

tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.002: Time is an immense subject. It contains history, breakfast, the age of stars, and the interval between deciding to add a snare and discovering it has landed on the wrong beat. The BPM screen addresses a modest portion of this territory: tempo, clock source, brightness and tap tempo. Everything else continues without a knob.
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.004: Open BPM for tempo, matrix brightness and the internal/external clock choice. Audio level lives under VOL → MAIN. The instrument allows you to see the beat more brightly without having to hear it more loudly, a distinction which neighbouring households may find particularly civilised.
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.005: A few colours which explain the relationship
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.008: TŒRN is master and sends clock as set in MIDI → SEND. Connected instruments may follow. An instrument which does not wish to follow should not be blamed on the grounds that the clock was sent very clearly.
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.014: J26 CLK-IN pulses advance play immediately, without waiting for lock, at MIDI → CIN’s PPQN. The number is measured tempo. The pulse has arrived; the instrument gets on with it.
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.018: The range is 40–300 BPM. For tap tempo, repeat taps on the appropriate pad here and allow the averaging to settle. A few clean taps are better than a large quantity of increasingly urgent ones. The computer averages the timings you supply, rather than the confident rhythm you were hearing inside your head.
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.019: A. An instrument which keeps its own time
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.020: Cyan digits and a green arrow pointing right identify internal master clock. Encoder 3’s ring is green. The machine has a time and is prepared to tell other machines about it. There is something rather endearing about this tiny electronic certainty, particularly in a universe where people can disagree about whether it is already too late for lunch.
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.030: EXT uses red < for TRS MIDI or orange < for J26 CLK-IN. Clicking from INT selects EXT on that source. This answers “which clock?” before the instrument is asked the rather more difficult question “where has the clock gone?”
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.033: B. An outside clock has become convincing
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.034: Green digits and a red left arrow mean incoming TRS MIDI is locked. The arrow blinks with the clock. Encoder 3 click moves to analog EXT, variant D. Encoder 4 changes the stored counter offset without replacing live clock. The instrument can keep a private correction while publicly agreeing to follow somebody else, a skill usually acquired only after several years in a band.
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.035: C. An outside clock has not yet made its case
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.036: Red digits and a red left arrow mean unsettled measurement or absent MIDI clock. Allow a few bars, then check the cable and master. Do not interpret the red display as impatience. It is a report, made with substantially less emotion than is likely to be invested in reading it.
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.037: D. Time arrives as a pulse
tempo-midi.html.tempo-midi.038: Orange digits and an orange left arrow show analog CLK-IN, with the arrow flashing on each pulse. Playback advances immediately; no green-lock wait is required. Set rate and hold-off in MIDI → CIN. Encoder 3 click returns to red < MIDI EXT. A pulse carries very little information, but can make a persuasive statement about now.

play.html.play.001: Other things the instrument is prepared to become
play.html.play.002: A device with one purpose is simple to explain and occasionally rather limiting. A device with many purposes can occupy a substantial amount of time explaining what it thought you wanted. TŒRN groups its alternatives under SETT for grid behaviour, MODE for performance and playback, and ETC → ADV for the display. Preview mode and volume are together under VOL → PREV. Encoder 4 takes you through the choices. You need not make all of them.
play.html.play.004: At the root, choose SETT and short-press encoder 4. Row 16 changes to the family colour; turning encoder 4 visits its siblings. Tap touch 2 to return to the grid. Reopening restores the parent family. This means that you can go in to adjust one small thing and come back out immediately, an entirely feasible course of action which the author recommends trying at least once.
play.html.play.005: SETT at the root. Here begins the discussion of how you thought the knobs ought to work.
play.html.play.006: A brief census of the alternatives
play.html.play.007: MODE offers FLOW, PMOD, LOOP, VMOD, CHLD, IMG, PONG, SONG, TCHY and AUTO. Open it with encoder 4, then select and press SONG to enter the arranger. ETC contains INFO, SD, BATT, ADV and RSET; ADV opens CRSR, LEDS, RAM, LGHT, COLR, EYES and FIRE. The last three names can give the impression that the instrument has acquired a face and an alarming hobby. They are display settings. It is worth establishing this before attempting to coax a tune out of the fire.
play.html.play.009: Choose MODE → TCHY, turn encoder 3 to ON, and leave with touch 1. The sequencer stops. Pads 1–5 now play sample voices 1–5 directly, one hit per touch; release a pad before hitting it again. Filters and effects remain in the path, but no notes are written to the pattern. You have acquired a five-pad instrument. This is a perfectly respectable musical development. The next thing to appear on the display is a flying Nyan Cat, and its connection with respectability is rather more difficult to defend.
play.html.play.010: The cat replaces the grid. Pads 1–5 give its frosting red, orange, green, blue and purple colours. A person encountering this without preparation might reasonably conclude that the more serious part of the manual had been misplaced. The sound engine continues to do its job. There is no technical requirement for every component of a musical instrument to have passed the same audition.
play.html.play.022: Hold to fast-record into the last voice played; release to finish. Its sample is replaced and its pattern notes remain. Identify the last voice before granting it a new recorded life.
play.html.play.026: Switch TOUCHY OFF, restore original channel volumes and open MODE in the menu. Leaving returns to the grid. The cat has gone elsewhere, as cats will.
play.html.play.027: Samples and filters still work as in Samples and Sound, returning to TOUCHY when you leave their screens. Pitch, reverb and highpass reuse voice settings; velocity is remembered per voice for the session. Switching TOUCHY OFF restores the original channel volumes. Reboot starts it OFF. Leaving does not restart playback automatically. These last provisions allow a performance to return to normal by a deliberate act, rather than by an instrument deciding that the interlude with the cat must surely be over by now.
play.html.play.028: Light which agrees with the beat
play.html.play.029: In darkness, a soft pulse across the grid can make the instrument look as though it is participating enthusiastically. In bright working conditions, it can make the note you are trying to edit rather harder to find. FLOW permits both observations to be acted upon.
play.html.play.031: ON adds the beat-synchronised wash. OFF leaves the playhead column alone. Choose the view in which you can most usefully understand what is happening.
play.html.play.035: Open VOL → PREV for the browser’s preview arrangements. Encoder 2 selects mode; encoder 3 sets volume 0–50. PREV stays above in the VOL colour. The lower orange number normally shows volume; a mode change shows ON, PRSS or SYNC for 2.5 seconds, then returns to the number. Encoder 2 and its hint are green, red or yellow respectively; encoder 3 remains orange. It is an elaborate presentation of a simple social question: is the next noise allowed to interrupt?
play.html.play.036: ON. Every highlighted file plays. This is efficient in a quiet room and an exciting way to browse a folder of alarming sounds through a large PA.
play.html.play.037: PRSS. Encoder 1 on a WAV grants an audition. It does not move up a folder. The sample has been asked to wait until introduced.
play.html.play.038: SYNC. During playback, the voice’s written hits audition the highlighted file. While stopped, encoder 4 auto-plays like ON. This lets you hear a sample in the company in which you expect it to work, rather than admiring it alone and discovering later that it gets on badly with everyone.
play.html.play.040: ON auditions selections automatically. PRSS waits for encoder 1. SYNC auditions automatically while stopped and substitutes the selected file on this voice’s pattern hits while running. The loaded voice is not muted; its triggers are skipped. One interview at a time.
play.html.play.043: How much of the pattern should be visible?
play.html.play.044: A page may be easier to edit alone. It may also become inexplicable without the neighbouring pages. VIEW is offered because both experiences can happen to the same person within a surprisingly short time.
play.html.play.046: EASY shows this page only. FULL shows it brightly with neighbours ghosted underneath. The ghosts are context, rather than evidence that a previous edit has come back to complain.
play.html.play.047: The page ends. Something must happen.
play.html.play.048: PMOD decides what follows a page and how a loop relates to the SONG arranger. The moment at which one thing ends and another ought to begin is central to musical structure, and has been the source of considerable difficulty for bands without a drummer.
play.html.play.059: Finish the page you started, even if the view moves elsewhere. At the boundary, play whichever page is visible. The instrument politely completes its current sentence before taking the hint.
play.html.play.063: The page colours and NEXT cueing are described in Song → pages & PMOD. You can inspect a destination without insisting that playback abandon the journey halfway there.
play.html.play.064: An outer boundary for the loop
play.html.play.065: LOOP sets the number of pattern pages before wrapping. OFF follows populated length. A repeated phrase needs an agreed end chiefly so that everybody knows which beginning to return to.
play.html.play.067: OFF follows the populated pattern. A number fixes how many pages play before wrapping. The existence of later material does not oblige the loop to visit it.
play.html.play.069: VMOD lets each voice loop through its own pages, with its pitches remaining attached to it. It is a modest-looking facility with the potential to produce the sort of pattern whose repetition seems always to be about to happen, then slips away by another beat.
play.html.play.072: A voice ends at its highest page containing notes. Empty voices do not extend the cycle; the pattern reaches as far as the longest voice. Each plays its own page at the common column and wraps independently. Conditions such as 1/2 and 1/4 count that voice’s wraps. Listen for a while. Different phrase lengths can create a larger rhythm which nobody explicitly wrote down, a pleasing example of arithmetic behaving as though it had been invited to improvise.
play.html.play.073: With VMOD on, FLOW, LOOP and pattern-mode page lock leave playback and page dots alone. Song mode is unchanged. The larger itinerary continues to exist outside these private calendars.
play.html.play.074: With CTRL = PAGE, encoder 2 visits pages containing the current voice. An empty voice keeps the full page range for its first notes. Changing voice takes you to its page. Encoder 4 does not switch pages while VMOD plays. This navigation can feel curious until you remember that a bassline and a hi-hat may now possess different ideas of where the phrase has got to.
play.html.play.075: White dots identify pages containing the voice selected by encoder 1. Green tracks that voice’s playing page, yellow the edit page. These colours spare you the task of holding several independent loops in your head while also deciding whether the snare is too loud.
play.html.play.076: MODE → IMG forces VMOD OFF and locks it there. Independent voice calendars and image painting use different arrangements of the same world.
play.html.play.077: A picture in which the colours make noises
play.html.play.078: IMG starts with a black matrix and paints using voices 1–8. The instrument has temporarily ceased pretending that a sound must live on its customary row. A picture can now become music for reasons its painter may understand only afterwards.
play.html.play.081: Ordinary row colours disappear. Painting a cell cycles through sample voices 1–8 and their colours. Touch 1 changes the brush voice without making a mark. Stay in DRAW; single mode is not used. You may find yourself adjusting the sound to improve the picture or the picture to improve the sound. Both are permitted, though they can make it unexpectedly difficult to answer the simple question “What are you working on?”
play.html.play.082: VMOD is forced OFF and REC → CLR is forced to FIX, preventing recording-related clears from unexpectedly removing the drawing. The instrument has made a small provision for the vulnerability of art to perfectly ordinary maintenance.
play.html.play.084: CTRL sets encoder 2’s normal duty in draw/single, outside special overlays. It is a useful decision to make before learning the wrong habit very thoroughly.
play.html.play.086: PAGE changes pages 1–16. VOL sets the cursor lane’s volume as a live fader. The difference becomes apparent as soon as you attempt to make the current page quieter.
play.html.play.089: LEDS tells the firmware what LED hardware is fitted. If the setting is wrong, pixels may be drawn beyond the visible area. This is an entirely comprehensible sort of darkness once you realise that the firmware believes the instrument is bigger than it is.
play.html.play.100: A small ball has its own musical method
play.html.play.101: PONG runs in draw and fires notes on muted voices only. Unmuted playback remains untouched. You have selected some notes not to be heard, and a ball is now visiting them selectively. This should be thought of as a performance option, rather than a considered criticism of your mute choices.
play.html.play.102: Speed on the left, ON on the right, a ball in the middle. The ball’s complete musical education is the geometry of the grid. It can nevertheless produce some results worth stealing.
play.html.play.105: The idle cartoon eyes are a separate animation, seen after inactivity while stopped. PONG needs draw with PONG ON. A ball making notes and a pair of eyes waiting for notes are two different answers to the question of what the instrument does when you leave it alone.
play.html.play.106: Finding the cursor without leaning over the instrument
play.html.play.107: Choose the appearance of the edit cursor. It is a small light with the important job of identifying which part of the composition your next mistake will affect.
play.html.play.109: NORM is a thin white ring. CHNR appears only on the focused voice in single. BIG supplies a 3×3 halo. With CHNR and CTRL = PAGE, encoder 2 flashes the page number at the right, one row below the top, without an underline. BIG is useful across a room, though operating the encoders from there remains your problem.
play.html.play.111: Use two hands with separate writing and erasing, or one-hand toggling. Full details are in Sequencing → Set & remove triggers. Human hands have been attached in roughly their present configuration for a considerable time. It seemed sensible to offer more than one way for them to approach the knobs.
play.html.play.113: L+R gives row selection and erase to encoder 1, placement to encoder 4. R gives toggling to encoder 4 and temporary full mute to encoder 1. Practise the new arrangement before attempting it in front of people who assume you already know which it is.
play.html.play.115: This mask selects which channels come back when encoder 3 leaves R mode’s temporary full mute. It does not restrict painting. The silence itself may be spontaneous; the notes which emerge from it can have been chosen rather carefully in advance.
play.html.play.116: Sixteen dots, channels 1–16. Green comes back unmuted; red remains silent. One can acquire an impressive degree of apparent spontaneity by preparing this list.
play.html.play.121: For example, bring back only kick and snare. The other parts can rejoin later, looking as though this was always the plan. See Sequencing → R mode.

midi.html.midi.002: Electronic instruments are spared a great many human misunderstandings. They do not sulk because the keyboard player has taken the last sandwich. They do not say “I was listening” while checking their telephone. In return, they have developed exact and frequently incompatible ideas about what a channel number means. The MIDI family establishes notes, transport, send and receive policy, overwriting, latency, analog clocks and selected-voice triggers before this precision becomes an obstacle to making music.
midi.html.midi.003: What can travel through which cable?
midi.html.midi.004: Musical MIDI uses the TRS ports. USB exposes a MIDI interface, but USB note, clock and transport handlers are not implemented here. USB audio remains available for recording the mix on a computer. This is a distinction worth making early. An interface can be visible to the operating system while possessing none of the conversational abilities you were hoping it would bring to the relationship.
midi.html.midi.005: Navigate the ten pages with encoder 4; most values use encoder 3. Combine with BPM → INT/EXT to decide master or follower. Once a common clock is established, the machines can disagree about notes with a much more impressive degree of punctuality.
midi.html.midi.006: MIDI at the root. The instrument is ready to hear what the other boxes have been trying to say.
midi.html.midi.007: The note and its intended recipient
midi.html.midi.008: An incoming note needs a voice. There are several quite sensible ways to choose it, and selecting a different sensible way from the one you expected is responsible for a remarkable variety of apparently nonsensical results.
midi.html.midi.010: Every incoming channel plays the voice selected by the grid’s Y position. The other instrument may believe it is playing the piano while you move the cursor to a sample of a door. Both machines are following their instructions impeccably.
midi.html.midi.014: KEYS is the legacy trigger map: C through G select sample voices 1–8 at base pitch, and G♯ through B also choose voice 8. The pitches are selectors here, rather than a tune the sampler has promised to reproduce.
midi.html.midi.017: Start, stop, and the possibility of continuing
midi.html.midi.025: Pair GET with EXT clock and SEND with INT. Two instruments both expecting to receive the instruction to start can wait together in perfect technical harmony for an extremely long time.
midi.html.midi.033: SEND has no separate OFF. Set note policy through RCVE, or relinquish master clock with BPM → EXT. In a conversation between machines, “stop talking” benefits from being qualified with what, exactly, should stop being said.
midi.html.midi.034: Whether the notes are allowed inside
midi.html.midi.039: A keyboard is larger than the picture of it
midi.html.midi.041: Fold incoming SEL/MIDI pitches by octaves into visible rows 1–15. Preview and playback use the visible pitch. The tune has been fitted into the instrument’s available height, a practical operation which can have musical consequences.
midi.html.midi.043: Keep the original MIDI pitch for preview, recording, playback and output. A folded visible row remains editable; moving it vertically transposes the stored pitch. The display is an address by which you can reach the note, rather than a complete declaration of where it sounds.
midi.html.midi.044: FOLD leaves the legacy KEYS mapping unchanged. It defaults ON and survives reboot. After returning to the instrument, remember to consider remembered settings among the possible explanations of what it is doing.
midi.html.midi.046: Two clocks can be in agreement while the actual sounds arrive slightly apart. A pair of kick drums is very good at explaining this failure, and will continue explaining it on every beat until somebody attends to SYNC. The offsets compensate latency in the outgoing and incoming paths.
midi.html.midi.051: Play both devices on the same downbeat and adjust SNC2 until the kicks coincide. If available, apply the matching negative to the other device’s send path. The aim is one attack. When it happens, an irritating technical problem simply vanishes into the entirely unremarkable experience of two things occurring together.
midi.html.midi.053: Analog clock uses separate two-pin headers. J25 CLK-OUT is 5 V; J26 CLK-IN accepts 3–5 V. On BPM, click encoder 3 to choose orange < analog input instead of red < MIDI. Pulse width is 1–50 ms, default 12. A pulse is about as short a statement as can usefully be made, which leaves very little room for correcting what the listener thinks it meant.
midi.html.midi.062: Rate 1 means one pulse per beat; 24 is classic Sync24-like density; 32 is denser than MIDI’s native 24 PPQN. The display follows width, STOP/CONT or ±rate, according to the last knob moved. This page governs output on J25. Input rate belongs under CIN. Decide which end of the conversation you are configuring before enthusiastically increasing its vocabulary.
midi.html.midi.063: Rev H headers: CLK-OUT(5V) is J25, CLK-IN(3–5V) J26, SIDEC-5V J27; see TRIG. Pin 1 is signal; pin 2 GND. Configure incoming clock under CIN. These are not MIDI DIN or line-level audio connections. The fact that signals can all be described as electrical does not make them interchangeable, any more than being written in ink makes two books the same story.
midi.html.midi.065: J27 SIDEC-5V outputs a 5 V trigger when the selected voice actually sounds. Width and polarity follow PPQN. This is for external equipment; it is not built-in sidechain compression. The instrument announces the occurrence. What the connected machine does about it is a separate matter to arrange.
midi.html.midi.069: CIN sets J26 CLK-IN. With orange < EXT selected on BPM, incoming pulses advance the sequencer. At 4 PPQN, every pulse is a step; at 24 PPQN, every sixth pulse is. Without this agreement, a perfectly regular clock can give the impression that the composition has suddenly become terribly impatient.
midi.html.midi.071: Hold-off rejects rises arriving too soon after the last counted pulse. Keep it below pulse spacing, or entirely respectable beats will find the door still closed.
midi.html.midi.073: Incoming pulses per quarter note. Default 4 gives a pulse per sixteenth, as with Volca. The number defines the distance between messages in musical time.
midi.html.midi.074: The display follows the last edit. Pin 38’s interrupt listens only in orange EXT; INT and MIDI EXT ignore CLK-IN. Press Play to begin on the next pulse. At 1 or 2 PPQN, a pulse covers four or two steps: the first happens immediately and the rest are spaced using the last pulse interval. The instrument spends those intervals predicting the future, a modest practical activity with a rather grand name.
midi.html.midi.075: Whether an arriving note may replace a resident one
midi.html.midi.077: Fill empty cells only. Existing notes, whether of this voice or another, keep their places. This default has prevented many enthusiastic incoming performances from becoming instant redevelopment projects.
midi.html.midi.080: Live input still sounds. OVWR controls what gets written during recording in SINGLE and survives reboot. A note may be heard quite clearly without being invited to stay.
midi.html.midi.081: Some arrangements which usually result in music
midi.html.midi.107: SEND has no OFF. Select CLCK for local play; an unplugged follower ignores clock which never reaches it. No further effort is needed to persuade an absent machine not to listen.

song.html.song.001: The loop is persuaded to leave home
song.html.song.002: A loop which works has very little incentive to become a song. It has a beginning, reaches an end, and finds its beginning waiting conveniently there again. Moving on means risking a bit which does not work quite so well. Song mode supplies a plan for this risk: 8 pages, PMOD, and a chain which can send playback somewhere new before it has time to become sentimental.
song.html.song.004: A pattern holds 256 steps, divided into 8 pages of 32 in the selected layout. The row-16 strip, explained in Matrix, reports which pages contain notes. MODE → PMOD chooses how they are visited. Simply having written several pages does not settle their order, any more than owning several destinations constitutes a holiday.
song.html.song.017: MODE → LOOP limits the sounding range, with OFF leaving the natural length. Short loops concentrate attention; longer ones allow a thought to develop. After several hours of work, it can become surprisingly difficult to distinguish a thought which is developing from a thought which has become comfortable and is considering ordering another drink.
song.html.song.019: Open MODE, turn encoder 4 to SONG and press. Up to 64 slots can point to the pattern’s 8 pages. With PMOD = SONG, playback follows the chain and wraps to the start. The arranger contains references to pages, rather than new copies of them. One page can therefore be given several appointments, while remaining the same page with the same hi-hat you are still meaning to fix.
song.html.song.020: Pattern page 07 in song slot 23. There are two numbers because “where is the material?” and “when shall we hear it?” turned out to be different questions.
song.html.song.024: Choose which page belongs in the selected slot. Its number uses the page’s voice colour. You can now decide what comes next without altering the material that will arrive.
song.html.song.030: Move the edit cursor through the chain. Row 1’s bright travelling dot marks the sounding slot. Editing and performing may consequently be at different points in the plan, which is often useful and occasionally an explanation of considerable surprise.
song.html.song.033: Set PMOD = SONG and enter SONG. Choose the slot with encoder 4, choose its page with encoder 2, then press encoder 2 or 4 to assign it. Repeat as required; empty slots are skipped. During playback, row 16 marks the sounding page and row 1 carries the green song-slot dot. Watch a complete pass before adding more structure. Sometimes an arrangement needs another section. Sometimes it needs the courage to stop returning to the previous one.
song.html.song.034: Put a page in three successive slots to play it three times, or alternate 01/02/01/02 for call-and-response. Repetition is one of music’s most powerful devices. It is also very good at concealing how long you have been meaning to write the next bit. The arranger accommodates both uses with equal efficiency.

menus.html.menus.001: A tree with buttons at the ends
menus.html.menus.002: The first difficulty with a menu is that you generally open it in order to do something else. The second is that, once inside, it offers you several other things which look interesting. This map exists to preserve a route back to the original intention. Blue identifies root families, red their nested leaves. For the actual appearance of a display, use the screen index. There is no prize for visiting every branch, although the afternoon may feel surprisingly short if you try.
menus.html.menus.004: Tap touch 2, the right pad, from the grid. Row 16 shows red and blue family dots; encoder 4’s green hint identifies the navigator. Submenus adopt the colour of their parent family. The colour is a useful thing to remember when the menu name has gone out of your head and all that remains is the feeling that you came in here for a reason.
menus.html.menus.006: There are ten root families. The short names below are exactly those printed by the matrix; indentation indicates depth. Some of the names look rather like words which have suffered minor transport damage. They are four-letter abbreviations. The descriptions restore enough of the missing language to let you decide whether this is the control you were looking for.
menus.html.menus.007: A note on the colours of maps
menus.html.menus.008: The handbook’s blue and red indicate nesting. They are not voice colours. The hardware uses the parent menu’s colour for submenu text. A useful map can differ considerably from the place it describes, provided it warns you which of its rivers are merely a convenient shade of blue.
menus.html.menus.009: Touch 2 opens the menu without stopping playback. Turn encoder 4 through the ten family dots on row 16; short-press to enter, and touch 2 to return to the grid. Reopen within five seconds and the last family is restored. Wait longer and you begin at PATT. Five seconds is the instrument’s estimate of the difference between a brief interruption and a new expedition. It is often rather shorter than the time it takes a person to remember what the brief interruption was.
menus.html.menus.010: One pattern slot stores all 8 pages, voices, step values and tone controls. Sample KIT selection remains separate. A pattern is a detailed account of what should happen, with certain assumptions about which noises will be available to make it happen.
menus.html.menus.011: NEW is PATT’s first entry. Loading an empty blue slot also opens it. Save before generating if the present RAM pattern matters. An empty file slot is not a request for the current tune to be remembered automatically.
menus.html.menus.012: The genre generator supplies a new RAM pattern and returns you to the grid. Available first in PATT and from empty slots. An effective treatment for the blank page, though a poor treatment for forgetting to save the page which was there before it.
menus.html.menus.013: The same settings roll differently each time. Randomness is most cooperative about the future and almost entirely unhelpful about reconstructing the recent past.
menus.html.menus.014: Choose the WAV kit for voices 1–8. Synths 11/13/14 remain unchanged and voices 9/10/12 remain empty. The same sequence may now mean something quite different.
menus.html.menus.015: SMP browses files for voices 1–8, also reached by touching both pads left-first on a sample row. Synth and empty rows show (−) and refuse entry. There is no recording behind those voices to browse, however thoroughly you ask.
menus.html.menus.016: The clock declares itself by colour and direction: cyan digits and green > for INT master; green digits and red < for locked MIDI EXT; red digits and red < while MIDI remains unsettled; orange digits and orange < for J26 analog input. It is a surprisingly diplomatic amount of explanation from something that is simply trying to say when.
menus.html.menus.017: Seven output leaves. Encoder 4 moves between them, encoder 3 usually adjusts the value; GAIN uses encoders 1–3. Begin with the lit cue. It is easier to make the right part louder if you first establish which part is presently being offered to you.
menus.html.menus.018: The 6.35 mm headphone level. The person most immediately affected by this setting is conveniently situated next to the knob.
menus.html.menus.019: Trim above fixed mix headroom. 1.0x is the old default, 2.0x doubles. ALL multiplies the other trims: 2.0x times 2.0x is four times the level. Neither factor knows that the other looked quite modest when you set it.
menus.html.menus.020: Applied at mixer1/mixer2 inputs and mixer_end synth send. 2-CH L+R retains 1–4, 5–8 and ALL; synths drop out. For a missing signal, follow the route before adjusting its volume.
menus.html.menus.021: Independent line-out trim. Loud headphones do not oblige the mixing desk to share the experience.
menus.html.menus.022: The browser’s preview policy and volume. An audition can be made to wait until everybody is ready.
menus.html.menus.023: Two channels, several arrangements of the sounds between them.
menus.html.menus.024: The actual routes are in Audio path → stereo out: OFF puts main and preview on both sides; M+P main left, preview right; L+R voices 1–4 left and 5–8 right, with synths omitted. Short labels benefit from long explanations on occasions like this.
menus.html.menus.025: The built-in speaker. A remarkably small object to entrust with an entire composition.
menus.html.menus.026: Turning off the speaker leaves the other output arrangements available. The little driver need not attend every performance.
menus.html.menus.027: Global GEQ treble cut. Useful for bright headphones and for the late stage of a session when every hi-hat appears to be standing slightly too close to your face.
menus.html.menus.028: The regular habits of grid view, encoder control, drawing and mute selection.
menus.html.menus.029: Choose how many surrounding notes remain in the picture while editing a page.
menus.html.menus.030: Encoder 2’s normal duty in draw/single, when no special mode has made another claim on it.
menus.html.menus.031: Remembered across reboot. The reason you chose it is not stored alongside it.
menus.html.menus.032: Distribute creation and erasure between the available hands.
menus.html.menus.033: Two-hand editing or one-hand toggling; see Sequencing → triggers. A change in method does not change the notes already written.
menus.html.menus.034: The channels which return when encoder 3 leaves R mode’s temporary full mute.
menus.html.menus.035: A kick-and-snare return is one option. It affects the comeback from silence, not which rows you may paint while everyone is present.
menus.html.menus.036: Input, gain, start behaviour and what survives a new take. The sound itself need only provide the interesting part.
menus.html.menus.037: Select the recording input before asking why the meter has heard nothing.
menus.html.menus.038: The selection determines whether MIC or L-IN gain matters.
menus.html.menus.039: The microphone preamp. Quiet events can be made large enough to keep.
menus.html.menus.040: Line trim, with coarser steps because the connected equipment is already supplying substantial level.
menus.html.menus.041: The point at which being ready becomes recording.
menus.html.menus.042: Choose the fate of the voice’s existing notes after its sample is replaced.
menus.html.menus.043: TRS MIDI and the analog timing and trigger headers. Several distinct means of arranging an appointment.
menus.html.menus.044: Give incoming notes a voice to speak through.
menus.html.menus.045: Start, stop and continue. A small vocabulary capable of controlling a large amount of activity.
menus.html.menus.046: Pair with BPM INT/EXT so that the transport and the clock agree about who is leading.
menus.html.menus.047: Select what leaves the MIDI output. The receiving instrument may have its own equally strong ideas about what should arrive.
menus.html.menus.048: No separate OFF. Use RCVE for note policy and BPM EXT to stop sending master clock as required.
menus.html.menus.049: Decide whether incoming notes should play the internal sound engines.
menus.html.menus.050: Fold SEL/MIDI pitches into the visible register, or preserve their original pitch.
menus.html.menus.051: Latency compensation: SNC1 for the send path, SNC2 for reception.
menus.html.menus.052: Adjust until two attacks sound like one. A correct setting is notable mainly for ceasing to attract attention.
menus.html.menus.053: J25 supplies 5 V CLK-OUT; J26 accepts 3–5 V CLK-IN. Both are independent of TRS MIDI.
menus.html.menus.054: Follow INT BPM or EXT MIDI/analog timing. Header details are in MIDI → PPQN.
menus.html.menus.055: Choose the voice which sends a pulse from J27 SIDEC-5V when it sounds.
menus.html.menus.056: Width and polarity follow PPQN. The output is a 5 V trigger, rather than a very short sample.
menus.html.menus.057: Set J26 input rate and hold-off. In orange EXT, pulses advance playback.
menus.html.menus.058: The controls resemble PPQN; connections are in MIDI → CIN. Similar controls do not give input and output the same job.
menus.html.menus.059: Whether incoming MIDI may replace notes already in occupied cells.
menus.html.menus.060: Open with encoder 4. MODE contains the alternatives to the instrument’s ordinary account of what it is doing.
menus.html.menus.061: The whole grid pulses with the beat. The lights take a more conspicuous interest in the performance.
menus.html.menus.062: Choose what happens when a page reaches its end.
menus.html.menus.063: Set a page count before the loop wraps. OFF follows the populated length.
menus.html.menus.064: Each page contains 32 steps in this layout. This is sufficient space for a great many intentions and their subsequent revisions.
menus.html.menus.065: Each voice loops through its own pages. Pitches remain with their voice.
menus.html.menus.066: FLOW, LOOP and pattern-mode page lock leave VMOD playback alone. Encoder 2 visits the voice’s filled pages; encoder 4 does not switch pages during play. Song remains unchanged. MODE → IMG forces VMOD OFF.
menus.html.menus.067: A simplified mode for small hands, whose confidence in buttons generally develops ahead of their interest in reading manuals.
menus.html.menus.068: There are fewer ways for an experiment to become a restoration job.
menus.html.menus.069: The matrix becomes a black canvas. Paint cycles sample voice colours.
menus.html.menus.070: Stay in DRAW for IMG. Single mode is not used. The picture has its own rules about what a row means.
menus.html.menus.071: A ball crosses draw mode and fires muted notes only. Unmuted playback remains as written. A modest intrusion into the parts you thought you had silenced.
menus.html.menus.072: The idle eyes are a separate animation. The ball has a performance role; the eyes are waiting for yours.
menus.html.menus.073: Sixty-four slots point at the pattern’s 8 pages. PMOD SONG follows the chain and wraps. Material and running order are stored as different things.
menus.html.menus.074: Empty slots are skipped. Row 16 shows the page; row 1’s green dot marks the song slot.
menus.html.menus.075: Five pads play five sample voices. Encoder 3 selects OFF/ON; touch 1 leaves the menu. A cat becomes involved for reasons which need not affect the music.
menus.html.menus.076: The companion studies voices, accents, velocities, harmony and BPM in a base range, then writes coordinated variations after it. Orange marks the source, green the destinations. It helps to identify which part of the pattern you are offering as advice and which part you are asking it to replace.
menus.html.menus.077: The engine is shared with single-mode randomize. An empty base produces a varied 4/4 starter ensemble. Repeated runs differ. The companion is extraordinarily patient about being asked whether it has any other ideas.
menus.html.menus.078: INFO, SD, battery status, ADV and RSET. Every substantial system eventually needs a place called “the other things.” Here the other things include both sleeping eyes and deletion of the entire session. Read the branch name.
menus.html.menus.079: Version first, then scrolling thanks. There were people behind all these lights.
menus.html.menus.080: Check the build before reporting a problem. An accurate version can spare somebody a long search through a bug’s previous lives.
menus.html.menus.081: USB serial access to the card. Remain on this page while the computer communicates.
menus.html.menus.082: If Connect reboots the unit, reopen SD. See SD card → SD tool. The connection can be recovered without removing the card or developing a theory about its motives.
menus.html.menus.083: An estimate of charge remaining. A battery has several hours of useful behaviour and then one rather uncompromising opinion about being empty.
menus.html.menus.084: Use USB-C before the red number becomes the complete absence of a number.
menus.html.menus.085: Display and diagnostic settings. Press encoder 4 to enter.
menus.html.menus.086: The cursor’s appearance, with options for eyes at different distances from it.
menus.html.menus.087: Identify the panel hardware actually fitted to the instrument.
menus.html.menus.088: Wrong geometry can put pixels outside the display. They have been drawn for a larger world than the hardware provides.
menus.html.menus.089: A live account of audio memory, from a pool of 96 blocks.
menus.html.menus.090: If A approaches 100 after a long session, clicks or distortion on mute/save may indicate exhausted blocks. This is a capacity problem, however much like an artistic decision it briefly sounds.
menus.html.menus.091: The optional LED strip around the chassis. Sometimes an enclosure wishes to make a contribution too.
menus.html.menus.092: Choose the colours by which you recognise the voices.
menus.html.menus.093: A stopped, idle instrument displays sleeping eyes. It has found something to do with being left alone.
menus.html.menus.094: Only while stopped on the grid. Any encoder or touch wakes it. The eyes make no claim about the internal experience of the processor.
menus.html.menus.095: A chosen voice’s white notes throw sideways embers which spread and fade. Gravity returns them towards the playhead. With sufficient patience it is possible to make the visual consequences of a single hi-hat rather more spectacular than the hi-hat.
menus.html.menus.096: The bar shows gravity left, colour right. Another encoder 3 click returns to voice selection. These controls adjust the sparks, which have no effect on the notes they appear to have escaped from.
menus.html.menus.097: Choose a reset with encoder 3, confirm with encoder 2, then wait for the green checkmark. The six options preserve different things. A short name should not be taken to imply a small consequence.
menus.html.menus.098: PATT and KIT delete saved material. These are poor buttons to press merely to see what happens.
menus.html.menus.099: If the shape of the screen is more familiar than its name, try the Screen index. It is the other way of navigating the instrument: by recognising what is there, rather than remembering what you thought you were going to do.

Each tile shows a menu or mode in its usual surroundings, with its name beneath. Select it to reach the explanation. There is no need to reconstruct how you got there. The specimen can be identified from its appearance.
